speechtext:

In how many government departments is it laid down that officials may not furnish direct to a member of parliament any statistical information requested by him (even though it be not of a nature "classified" on security grounds) but must channel it through the minister's office or some other such intermediary?

maintopic: * STATISTICAL INFORMATION TO MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
This is a question which is marked as one which the hon. member wishes to have answered orally. There is not, and I do not know that there has ever been, any general directive of the character

described in the question, and applying to all departments. Each minister has the responsibility for the administration of his own department and generally is looked upon as having the responsibility for any information that comes from that department.
Of course there are some matters about which inquiries can be made, that require merely statements of fact, that are not open to any controversy whatsoever. They are actual facts. R. F. WELCH CONSTRUCTION COMPANY
speechtext:
1.	Has the R. F. Welch Construction Company (British Columbia) Limited, since April 1, commenced work by extra gangs on the Calgary division of the Canadian National Railways?
2.	If so, how many men are employed on each of such extra gangs?
3.	Has the said company been requested by the brotherhood of maintenance of way employees to hire sectionmen and B & B men who are for the moment laid off as regular Canadian National Railway employees on said gangs?
4.	If so, how many of sectionmen and B & B men laid off by the railroad company have been taken on the strength of the said gangs by the said construction company?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Transport
maintopic: R. F. WELCH CONSTRUCTION COMPANY
speechtext:
The Canadian
National Railways advise as follows: -
1.	On April 1 and 2 two gangs commenced work on the Calgary division, which was completed on April 25.
Since the first of the year R. F. Welch (B.C.) Limited has also had a small gang of 12 to 15 men doing miscellaneous work on the Calgary division. For the purpose of unloading steel rails this gang was later increased to about 22 men of whom 16 were immigrants brought to Canada by R. F. Welch (B.C.) Limited during the early summer of 1954 and are still employed by that company.
2.	Gang No. 1, set up on April 1, consisted of 73 men, of whom 61 were labourers employed by R. F. Welch (B.C.) Limited and 12 were Canadian National Railways maintenance of way employees, comprising foremen and machine operators recruited from the regular maintenance of way section forces.
Gang No. 2, set up on April 2, consisted of 70 men, of whom 58 were labourers employed by R. F. Welch (B.C.) Limited and 12 were Canadian National Railways maintenance of way employees, comprising foremen and machine operators recruited from regular section gangs.
3 and 4. So far as the management is aware R. F. Welch (B.C.) Limited has not been requested by the brotherhood of maintenance of way employees to hire sectionmen and B and B men who are for the moment laid off as regular Canadian National Railways employees on said gangs. However, there always has been an understanding with the Welch organization that laid off railway maintenance of way employees will be given preference in employment on Welch gangs. Moreover, roadmasters have been instructed to provide the employment office with names
of laid off men wishing to work on Welch gangs, and these men receive preference.
Only a few laid off maintenance of way employees are known to have accepted work on the Welch gangs. During the past month (April) there has been an actual shortage of sectionmen and since April 15 requests have been placed with the Calgary office of the national employment service for extra men to fill the requirements of railway section gangs on the Calgary division. Of the men employed on the three gangs above referred to 125 were recruited through the Edmonton office of the national employment service.

maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
subsubtopic: REGARDING EXPLOSION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of National Defence. Is the minister in a position to make a statement regarding the explosion at Valcartier Camp late last night, and the death of three persons following it?

speakeroldname: Hon. R. O. Campney (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
subsubtopic: REGARDING EXPLOSION
speechtext:
I have just received a report on this accident, Mr. Speaker, and I think it covers most of the salient facts.
Last evening a party of four civilians, two men and two women, entered a road leading from the Camp Valcartier-Valcartier village road to the back of Valcartier Camp. They drove their car to a double row of large fence posts which had been placed across the road to prevent entry to the area, which is a rocket range and is out of bounds to all civilians. The telephone poles along the road are clearly marked "out of bounds". At both ends of the road there are signs marking the fact that it is national defence property. The range itself is clearly marked with large signs in both English and French reading, "danger, unexploded projectiles".
Notwithstanding these warnings, this party of four people parked their car at the double row of fence posts and went approximately one-quarter of a mile into the range beyond the fence posts and there began collecting inert rocket bombs on the range. After apparently loading the car with some 40 or 50 of these, it was found that the weight was too great for the vehicle. Accordingly some of the rockets were thrown onto the ground to lighten the weight; at least the lady

who was injured so indicated. One rocket exploded when thrown out and three of the occupants of the car, namely Mr. O. P. Daigle, Mr. Adrian Labranche and Miss Marie Clare-Daigle were killed. Mrs. O. P. Daigle was severely injured, but was able to walk to the camp, a distance of some two and a half miles, where she called at the first house where she saw a light shining. It happened to be the home of the medical officer, who immediately arranged for her to be taken to a hospital in Quebec city. The provost corps, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and the provincial police were immediately summoned and a full investigation is now under way.

maintopic: NATIONAL REVENUE

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Prime Minister. In view of the concern of all of us, will the Prime Minister, on behalf of this house, personally investigate every aspect of the McCann-Drohan-Demp-sey-Frost affair to ascertain whether or not the Minister of National Revenue acted in complete accordance with his responsibilities as a minister?
Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime
Minister): Mr. Speaker, I do not think I should personally investigate an incident that seems to be of considerable partisan political importance in the course of the election that is taking place in the province of Ontario at this time. I am satisfied that the Minister of National Revenue has discharged his duties in accordance with the practice that has prevailed hitherto. I do not want to get into any controversy about it.
The hon. gentleman asked me whether I was going to make a personal investigation of the facts. I have heard the denial of the rumours that have circulated about the way this incident took place, and having ascertained from the Minister of National Revenue what actually did take place I do not think I need make any further examination of the problem.

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: NATIONAL REVENUE
subtopic: ALLEGED RELEASE OF INFORMATION-REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a supplementary question. So that any misunderstanding may be avoided, because I might say it is our intention to defer an examination of this subject until the estimates of the minister are before the house and we can discuss it with a freedom that is not possible now, do I understand

Inquiries of the Ministry from the statement of the Prime Minister that he is fully informed in regard to the facts of this case in reaching the decision which he has stated?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: NATIONAL REVENUE
subtopic: ALLEGED RELEASE OF INFORMATION-REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: All I can say is that I am fully informed in respect of the information that has been given to me. I cannot say there is no information other than that which I have received that might be given to me. I have formed my opinion on the information I have received, and I feel satisfied that it fully covered the incident.

maintopic: NATIONAL REVENUE
subtopic: ALLEGED RELEASE OF INFORMATION-REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a supplementary question of the Prime Minister. Following the examination he made, does he not consider that it is a matter of impropriety, or at least an action that is apt to give rise to serious consequences, when a minister of the crown holding a portfolio is also a director of a company that deals with that department?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: NATIONAL REVENUE
subtopic: ALLEGED RELEASE OF INFORMATION-REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I understand the Minister of National Revenue has been connected with this company, or with one of its predecessors that is being continued by the company under the present name, for some 42 years. He was Minister of National Revenue when I became Prime Minister, and I was very happy to have him continue because I knew of the efficient and painstaking way in which he had handled the responsibilities of that department, and I have never had any occasion to find any clash between his duties as the Minister of National Revenue and whatever connection he might have with this company, which I do not know has relations with the Department of National Revenue.

maintopic: NATIONAL REVENUE
subtopic: ALLEGED RELEASE OF INFORMATION-REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: I should like to ask a supplementary question. I do not think that answers the situation at all. Is this not the type of case which indicates that no minister should hold a directorship while a member of the government?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: NATIONAL REVENUE
subtopic: ALLEGED RELEASE OF INFORMATION-REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
That is a matter about which I inquired before I became a member of the government, and I was told there was no rule of law or even traditional practice that required anyone who accepted such responsibilities to sever any previous connections he might have had. I was told that was something for each individual to consider in respect of his own position, and he might feel that it was desirable to sever all connections. In fact I felt that it was desirable to sever all such connections to avoid occasions for the kind of criticism-which I feel is not justified-that is being directed against the Minister of National Revenue at the present time.

I felt that I should not accept the invitation which was extended to me to become a member of the government unless I did sever my connections with the commercial and industrial firms with which I had been connected previously, but that is a matter each one has to decide for himself. I am sure that each one when he takes office does his best to fully discharge the responsibilities implied in his oath of office.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: NATIONAL REVENUE
subtopic: ALLEGED RELEASE OF INFORMATION-REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that the principles being enunciated by the Prime Minister are of importance beyond the case mentioned, would the Prime Minister tell us whom it was that he referred to when he was told about this position?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: NATIONAL REVENUE
subtopic: ALLEGED RELEASE OF INFORMATION-REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
I was invited by the then prime minister, the late Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, to become a member of his government. In the course of conversation I asked him about this and he told me there was no legal rule nor any traditional rule established by practice that would require me to sever my connections with the companies with which I had been associated; that that was a matter for each one to consider in the light of the position he would be assuming in becoming a member of the government.
I realized that there could be occasions for criticism, because in spite of my resignations it was suggested in this house that I had agreed to become a minister in order to carry out policies which were those of a board of directors with which I had been associated previously. In order to dispel that suggestion I had to assert in the house that the policy referred to in the criticism that was being made had never been mentioned in any way in the deliberations of that board, and that I had in fact severed my connections with that board before taking my oath of office.
In political life one must expect that any circumstance can be seized upon to direct what is frequently unfair criticism against those who hold office, and I wanted to leave as few opportunities as possible for unfair criticism.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: NATIONAL REVENUE
subtopic: ALLEGED RELEASE OF INFORMATION-REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question, to have the record complete? In view of the fact that the Prime Minister did resign all his directorships within a week after being sworn in as a member of the privy council, does he not think his colleagues should follow his lead?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: NATIONAL REVENUE
subtopic: ALLEGED RELEASE OF INFORMATION-REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
I do not think for the conscience of any others; I respect their concern for their responsibilities and reputations when they become members of the government. Each one has to make his own appraisal

of what it is advisable for him to do in order to have his position as honourably regarded as possible.

Mr. Speaker, just previous to my return to the house this afternoon there was an interparty meeting on the steps of the parliament building, and it was suggested by some of my Liberal friends and one of my C.C.F. friends that I would make myself highly 50433-233i

However, after discussing it with the members of one of the other groups we decided that as it is so hard to get the Liberals to understand things we should repeat, repeat and repeat them. In the few minutes at my disposal yesterday I indicated that I supported fully what the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Patterson) had said in respect to fisheries in British Columbia. I mentioned something about the autocratic minister; and while I did not say so at that time, I must say now that I think possibly he is really a good man to send to Russia. One dictator would meet another.
First I should like to discuss the effect of the conservation methods which were formerly employed and what their results have been. On September 17 the fisheries council of Canada issued a bulletin. In that bulletin they referred to the question of whether Hell's Gate paid off. I am not very much ii. ^rested in how well Hell's Gate paid off, becu 'se this is not only the question of a means f promoting a dam, but of a conservation me '"re that was carried out at that time, the same type of conservation to which I am proposing we return. If Hell's Gate paid off, the conservation measure which was employed at that time necessarily must have played an important part in it. Part of this, report says:
Canadian and American fishermen are expected to take over 10 million fish from the 1954 Adams river run which is now being fished by the gill netters in the Fraser river. This is a quite different picture from the "flop" in 1950, although 1946, the previous cycle year, was very good.
. . . the results of conservation and regulation are impressive and it is gratifying that the press has devoted so much space to it since it will make it easier in future to secure funds for this type of work.

speechtext:
An hon. member has suggested taking it up under the fisheries department estimates. I had not decided how long I would speak on this matter, but he has just about made up my mind to spend my full time on it and possibly speak on it under the fisheries estimates and under supply as well, if he wishes.
The question arises as to who conserved these fish that made it possible for us to have
3692	HOUSE OF COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Hahn in 1954 the biggest fishing season in the history of the Pacific coast. It is apparent that it was the former action on conservation that made this possible. Here we had a group of fishermen who for years, with the assistance of the Department of Fisheries, had helped to conserve the fish in the Fraser river and made this huge catch possible. I say it is rather ironic, and certainly it is not right, that these fishermen, after they have conserved all these fish for all these years, should now be forced to put out to sea, much against their own wishes. The conservation program made it possible to protect the fishing industry and has given us the greatest season for fishermen in recent years.
On November 16 Mr. A. J. Whitmore, the chief supervisor of fisheries, issued a statement regarding Fraser river chum salmon fishing for 1954. At that time he said:
(1) Chum salmon fishing operations, both gill net and purse seine, have been intensive in the outside approaches to the Fraser, particularly the Johnstone strait area.
Section 3 goes on to say:
The main run of chums in the Fraser area normally occurs during the month of November. Surveys of spawning streams in the lower Fraser during the past few days show that they are practically devoid of chum salmon spawners from this main run.
That is a very pertinent statement, especially in view of the fact that we had begun in a modified way to put into practice the closure that was suggested last year by the minister. The escapement was not what the department had hoped for. It goes on to say:
The only chum escapement of significance so far has come from the early run which passed through the fishing area several weeks ago.
That was prior to the closure. Section 5 goes on to say:
To assist in meeting conservation requirements, it is therefore considered necessary that the period of the approaching weekly close season be extended from a three-day period to a five-day period . . . that all net fishing be closed commencing at 8.00 a.m. Thursday, November 18, to 8.00 a.m. Tuesday, November 23.
They have had to change the regulations as a direct result of their policy, which was not doing the job it was intended to do. One week later, on November 24 of last year, another bulletin was issued by the same man. I would direct the minister's attention to sections 1, 2, 4 and 7 of this report. No. 1 says in part:
It had been expected that considerable numbers of chum salmon would have escaped to the spawning grounds during the five-day closure in effect last week end. Further surveys, however, during the past week, do not show this to be the case.

So this additional closure did not help at all. Section 2 states:
The numbers of spawners visible on the grounds* at this time are alarmingly few; the smallest for a considerable number of years despite the closure of fishing above the New Westminster bridge for a considerable part of the season.
Here we have a condemnation by the fisheries department's own man of the policy that was set up last year. Despite the closure of fishing above New Westminster bridge for a considerable part of the season there were fewer spawners there than for the past several years. Then section 4 states:
Catches by commercial fishermen in the river below the New Westminster bridge and by Indians in the up-river area have been practically nil, indicating that there are very few spawning fish escaping past the commercial fishery.
We certainly cannot blame the fishermen on the Fraser river for being responsible for that condition at this time. Section 7 states:
It is, therefore, considered essential that all salmon net fishing in district No. 1, including Howe sound and Burrard inlet, be discontinued as from 8.00 a.m. Friday next, November 26, 1954, in the interests of conservation.
It was therefore found necessary to completely close the area to fishing until such time as we could get the fish up on the spawning grounds and provide for future fishing. That is the absolute opposite to what we found was true in former years when, through co-operation between the fishermen themselves and the Department of Fisheries, it was possible to conserve sufficient fish to build up the fisheries industry to the point where we find it today.
Later, on March 16 of this year-just two months ago-Mr. Whitmore issued another bulletin in respect to the salmon spawning report for 1954. On the first page of that he had this to say:
Developments ox special interest associated with the 1954 salmon migration and spawning escapement showed continuing improvement in the volume and distribution of sockeye spawning stocks in the Fraser.
Later in section 4 he says:
Fishing efficiency in the Johnstone strait and Discovery passage area is regarded as the major factor responsible for the light escapement of chum spawners to streams on the lower mainland coast, including those of Jervis inlet, Pender harbour, Howe sound, and Fraser river areas.
Just as it says, that would indicate that fishing efficiency is the major factor responsible for the fewer spawning fish going up the river. Then on page 2, there is a paragraph under the heading of spring salmon. This escapement I am speaking of now occurred while the upper Fraser fishing was going on in full swing. That is, in the spring escapement the fishing was being carried

on at the time the spring salmon were making their way up the river. It goes on to say this:
Spawning stocks of this species over the province were well maintained. The escapement of springs to the Fraser watershed was satisfactory; well up to average in the Kamloops, Quesnel and Prince George areas, and above brood year levels in the Chilliwack and Harrison areas.
So you see that when the spring salmon were permitted to escape while the fishing was being done on the Fraser river according to the regulations as set forth by the Department of Fisheries in co-operation with the gill net fishermen on the Fraser, a sufficient number of spring salmon made their escapement. It was only during the time we found the fishing period changed that we ran into trouble.
Then in his statement in respect to chums on page 3, at the time of escapement of chums the fishing season was closed to the fishermen above New Westminster bridge. Let us see what effect it had:
The over-all catch of chums was above average and with the exception of district No. 1 spawning supplies generally were satisfactory.
District No. 1 is the Fraser river district. With that exception, spawning in that area or in the over-all picture was satisfactory. This fact would indicate again that the argument that the closure of the Fraser river is in any way going to help in the matter of conservation of salmon at this time is not valid.
Let us analyse the reason for the effects of the closure as we now have it before us. The minister closed the fishing, that is above the Pattullo bridge, and after it was closed we lost spawning fish. The reason is quite apparent. If one were to stand on Pattullo bridge and look down the river, one could see the twinkle of many hundreds of lights on boats on the river. Just as we had earlier forecast, the fishermen merely went down river; and where we had a few hundred boats there before we added this huge number that had been up river up to that time. So we just doubled the number of fishermen below Pattullo bridge. I perhaps should not say "doubled", but rather that we increased the number of fishermen below Pattullo bridge. That merely meant the same number or more fish would be caught, for they could not get around the boats so well and the chances of fish escaping through the network of boats and nets were practically nil.
Then of course there was another factor, namely that more intensified fishing was carried on in outside waters, as the minister had suggested in his 1953 address to the
The Budget-Mr. Hahn fishermen's union. These fishermen were certainly doing an excellent job of netting them as they came around Vancouver island and into the Fraser.
Another reason for this closure not having the effect that it was suggested it should have is that only 1 per cent of the salmon are caught in that region above the bridge as compared with the other area, and it naturally could not have the effect that was hoped for.
What does this closure mean to the people of the area? The hon. member for Fraser Valley indicated something of that in his address yesterday, but I would say this. First, it means that those who were normally catching fish on the Fraser are now obliged to catch the same number, if possible, out at sea. This means that there is added cost to the fishermen. So the cost of fishing to these people is more. It means that a good number of these 600 and more fishermen in the area naturally enough do not have the equipment to go out to sea; therefore they just aggravate the unemployment condition in the area. It also means that community business suffers. The return to the fishermen will be less and therefore they would not have the money to spend in the community. It also means that those fishermen who were set up under the Veterans Land Act and who supplemented their income by getting something from this fisheries industry are being deprived of what had been their right for a good number of years.
There is one pathetic factor involved here, and that is that these same fishermen are not eligible for unemployment insurance. When they are in need and require financial help, they just do not get it.
At this time, Mr. Speaker, I should like to bring to the attention of the minister a letter I received in reply to one I had written to Mr. Fred Rolley, secretary of the Pacific fishermen and allied trades union, gill net section. I think this is quite self-explanatory and needs little comment on my part:
Dear Sir:
Replying to your letter of February 8 asking for certain information as to the income of the fishermen of the upper Fraser, we have done our best in the time at our disposal to get you some information in this matter.
We have taken a cross section that we think would be average, neither the best or the worst of the fishermen and placed them in two categories, the first group containing an average cross section of full time fishermen who fished entirely above New Westminster bridge in both 1953 and 1954. The fishing effort of this group would be over a period of nine months in 1953 and eight months in 1954.

The story of the fisheries among these people on the Fraser river is sad. They have all had their incomes cut very materially. I know the minister can argue that these fellows are not real fishermen, and that if they went to sea they would get seasick. Possibly they would, but it does not necessarily mean a man is not a fisherman because he cannot go to sea. These men have been fishing on the river for years and making a living. They have conserved the fish over the years, and they see no reason why they should be deprived of that privilege. We might just as well argue that an airplane pilot is not a pilot if he happens to black out in the course of a dive. That does not mean he cannot fly an airplane.
These fishermen can fish. They have proven their ability to fish, as indicated in the letter from which I read. In some instances they have earned up to $5,000; and to be cut down to well below $2,700 because of the fisheries policy is not fair to the men in that area.
Is there a place for both seine and gill net fisheries on the Pacific coast? Certainly there is. The fishermen are agreed there is. All these men, no matter who they are, agree that the fishermen in the seine boats can carry on their fishing at sea and at the same time fish in the Fraser river can be conserved through the method in effect until last year. The answer is progressive closure in the early season to permit the salmon to go on up the river unmolested.
I said a good deal about the quality of fish in my speech on this subject on February 2 of this year. It can be found on page 778 of Hansard. I am not going to repeat what I said at that time, but I would suggest that


the minister take note of it. Another question has arisen quite recently in which I think the minister might be interested. It has to do with the problem of the conservation of fish on an international basis. Just prior to the opening of the house after the Easter recess, in fact on the Sunday before, the united fishermen and allied workers' union called a meeting of all interested United States and Canadian fishermen to discuss the problem of conservation.
I think that organization should be given some credit for its foresight in taking action at that time. To indicate who were there and that it was not a meeting of Canadian organizations only, I find in the minutes such names as Dan Assu, vice president, southern district, native brotherhood of British Columbia; H. Steve Stavenes, president of the united fishermen and allied workers' union; John Brown, president of the reef netter owners' association; Floyd Gregor, president of the reef netters' union, local 4 of the international longshoremen's workmen's union; Bob Cummings, secretary of local 3, international longshoremen's workmen's union; Joe Burrows, president of the Puget Sound gill netters' association; Lud Bretvich, vice president of the Puget Sound gill netters' association; and Dick Kink of the Puget Sound vessel owners' association.
I had been invited to the meeting, as was the minister. The minister could not attend, but I do not blame him for not being in attendance because he might have been asked for a policy statement which I do not think could properly have been made there. However, I did note with satisfaction that the minister had representatives at the meeting. For some time now it has been suggested that such a committee should be set up to study the problem of conservation.
I should like to compliment the minister at this point on having the foresight to suggest to the fishermen of British Columbia last year that they go out to sea off Vancouver island, do their fishing there and get their fish before the Americans got theirs. The salmon run through that water, and by doing that the United States fishermen would have their catches cut so much they would come to terms. Apparently they are ready to act, for the fishermen themselves do not want a race to deplete the fisheries industry.
As a result of that meeting a resolution was moved which I should like to put on record at this time. It is to be found on page 7 of the minutes, and reads as follows:
This joint conference recommends to all fishermen's organizations and all other interested fishery-organizations on both sides of the international boundary that the proposal of the U.F.A.W.U. for the inclusion of pink salmon into the jurisdiction

of the international Pacific salmon fisheries commission for conservation, rehabilitation and equal division be given thorough study and support.
Be it further resolved all organizations represented here agree to hold further joint conferences at the request of organizations on either side of the line as soon as possible in order to work out the maximum unity and to agree on steps to implement whatever common program is adopted.
The minutes continue as follows:
The resolution was seconded from the floor and brother Bob Cummings of the I.L.W.U. spoke in favour of the resolution.
It will be noted on page 8 of the minutes that the resolution was put to a vote and carried unanimously. All the people who were there representing these various organizations were unanimous with respect to handling this fisheries problem we have in the Pacific northwest. I would particularly commend to the minister's attention the proposal that the international Pacific salmon fisheries commission should proceed to look after the existing problem. I am not alone in this suggestion. The British Columbian, a newspaper which speaks for the people of that area, had this to say in an editorial headed "Fishermen's Voice" in its issue of April 19, 1955:
Success of the work of the international Pacific salmon fisheries commission, which governs the catch and distribution of the sockeye salmon, should be enough to encourage the governments of Canada and the United States to work out a similar treaty on pink salmon.
Need of the treaty, to end a continuing battle between the fishermen of the two nations, is indicated by the strength of the voice of the fishermen at the week end.
American boats have long held the balance of power because of a larger fleet but as Canada's fleet grows the need of a treaty becomes more urgent. Organization and control of the fleets, protection of the runs by a commission established through a treaty will be necessary to maintain this important part of the salmon fishing industry. What the international Pacific salmon fisheries commission achieved for the sockeye-that is, fair distribution of the catches through adequate controls, building up of the runs through control and conservation, and a general elevation of the tasty sockeye itself-can be done for the secondary pink salmon.
The voice of the fishermen meeting at White Bock was loud enough to be heard at Ottawa and Washington, and should produce results.
I ask only that the minister take note of that fact, that this is a desirable thing, and I would ask him to support the fishermen's unions in this request.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this has been a long debate, and I had not intended to take part in it. However, I shall speak for only a few moments.
In rising to speak may I say that I feel I have some prescriptive right, if I may put it that way, because I would remind the house that for about a year I had asked the minister of finance to reduce the excise tax
The Budget-Miss Bennett on automobiles. Of course I was very happy, along with all members in the house and the people of Canada generally, to see a reduction. But may I say, with all due respect to the minister, that I think he should have gone further. I believe there should have been a full reduction of this 15 per cent tax, commonly described as a luxury tax.
One of my reasons for saying this is that not many weeks ago the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) said in the house that the upswing in business and employment in the United States was in no small measure due to the upswing in the automotive industry, and the increased production in that industry. What is true of that country would be equally true of this. I am told further that if the tax were removed entirely we would be able to produce cars in Canada as cheaply as they do in the United States. This would mean a tremendous increase and widening of the market for motor cars.
Singling out this industry in particular, it must be kept in mind that considering it in its primary stage, which is the production of motor cars, and also in its secondary stage, its tertiary stage, and all its other ramifications, the automotive industry is the largest employer of men and women in Canada. That means a great deal. It means that it is the largest producer of homes and of food and all those things required to maintain the population of this country. We must also keep in mind that not only is this a very important industry, but that at least 179 other industries in this nation are entirely dependent upon the production of automobiles. These various industries stretch from coast to coast, from the Atlantic to the Pacific. They provide work and homes and all those things the employees require.
When one stops to consider the amount of steel, iron, aluminum, rubber, oil, textiles and products of the farm that are used in the manufacture of motor cars and all their component parts, and thinks at the same time of the farmers who receive additional income, one realizes just how important it is. Just think of the employees in the steel industry, the aluminum industry, the oil industry and the textile industry who need support and assistance at this time. I note the minister has just now entered the chamber, and I trust he will give this matter sound and diligent thought and consideration, to ascertain whether it would not be advisable, right at this time when we have unemployment in somewhat serious proportions, to consider entirely removing the 15 per cent excise tax from automobiles.

The Budget-Miss Bennett
I believe the country would benefit from such action. I believe the treasury would benefit by way of additional sales, additional employment and additional taxation. Sometimes I think we lose sight of the fact that 90 per cent of the men and women driving cars in Canada are earning $3,000 a year or less. This means that 90 per cent of the men and women driving cars are on salaries in the lower brackets. They are the men and women who are moving from place to place, maintaining the mobility of labour. It was not so many weeks ago the Minister of Labour mentioned the fact that the mobility of labour in this country meant a great deal in maintaining the level of employment. We would greatly increase the numbers of car buyers if the prices of automobiles could be reduced through a further reduction in the tax.
I know the country must collect taxes; but it may be that we are at the point of diminishing return so far as the automotive industry is concerned. In my view the additional revenue that would come to the minister from other industries by way of income tax would more than compensate him. I venture to say he would be further ahead if the excise tax were removed, and in the meantime it is almost certain that several thousand more people would be given employment. When I say that I think I am speaking very conservatively.
I have said I would be brief, but there are one or two further comments I have to make, the first of which has to do with the royal commission the minister announced. I do hope that when it is appointed careful consideration will be given to processing our raw materials into finished products. I am sure it is correct to say that we are 25 or 50 years behind the times in this. respect. We are still directing our economy along the lines we followed when we were a young country, when we had tremendous resources which, it was felt, could never be exploited. In those days we had a small population and it was all right to send out our raw materials and allow some other country to process them.
But what has happened? Our supplies of iron ore are running out, and the same applies to our supplies of aluminum. The same can be said about our nickel and copper. All these are going to the United States to be processed. One outstanding example I would place before the minister for his consideration is that of asbestos fibre. Canada sells $60 million worth of asbestos fibre to the United States each year. In that country our asbestos is processed and turned into 
finished products for resale. The result is that the $60 million becomes $450 million in the United States.
Think of the homes that sum of money provides. Think of the building it makes possible. Think of the clothes and the food, the extent to which all concerned along the line benefit by this $450 million. I say we have arrived at a stage in this country when we must keep those raw materials within our own borders, and give to our men and women the benefit of the returns that can be obtained from those materials, and the labour opportunities that would be opened up.
Then I have one further point-it seems that I keep on saying I have one more statement to make-and this has to do with immigration. I hope the royal commission will consider immigration so we may have some over-all plan. This is a great and magnificent country. It can be said that in the last 50 years in particular the very foundations of what we have in Canada today, industrially, economically, socially and indeed morally, were laid by the newcomers to this nation, those who went out to our frontiers and opened up our farms, our mines, our forests and our fisheries. We should have some overall plan under which new people coming to this country would go to our frontiers, would man our new lands, would go to our mines, our fisheries and our forest industry.
What really is happening now, and it is a rather serious thing, is this. We see it down in the older parts of Ontario, particularly in the north of my county where a great deal of farming is carried on. These newcomers come in and they go on the farms. They stay there only a short time. Then what happens? They leave and go into the cities, into the crowded industrial areas, and there they try to find employment. During last year they helped to swell the ranks of the unemployed. The farmers are not really able to depend on their staying during the season when they need them most.
Therefore in this country we should adopt some real over-all plan under which these new people coming in will go out and make themselves worthy citizens, which they want to do, and at the same time further expand, extend and exploit this great land to the extent that it should be exploited.
This is the last point, Mr. Speaker. A great many things have been said in this debate, and they did not always refer to finance. This is becoming a very dangerous country in which to live. The other night the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Studer) more or less raised a battle cry in this house. He said the gentlemen of the house should wear beards to protect themselves, I guess, against the women, to whom

he referred in not too complimentary terms, as I recall it. He said we have four women sitting in the house right now.
Well, you know, we have had a great many conflicts in this house, Mr. Speaker, over the years, many historic conflicts, but now we are about to have the greatest conflict of them all. I look across the house, I look to my left and I look to my right and I think of all these great men, such as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) himself and perhaps the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) who just went out. I can just visualize how they would look with beards. You know, Mr. Speaker, I shudder to think what is going to happen with respect to dislocation of industry. For example, barbers will be out of employment. Then the steel makers will be on short time, too, because they will not be making razors. The soap makers will be on short time because they will not be making soap powder and soap, or whatever these gentlemen use on their faces, to say nothing of the perfumeries. All these gentlemen use perfume and put these lotions on their faces, but sometimes you cannot tell whether it is a shaving lotion or what it is.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we are going to have a tremendous displacement of industry just because the men of this house want to make themselves into Goliaths; they want to be Samsons. Let me remind them, before they embark on this venture, that for every Goliath there is a David and for every Samson there is a Delilah.

speechtext:
A few
days ago, on the orders of the day, I asked the Minister of National Revenue a very simple question. I asked whether he would make a statement to the house that would clarify his position with regard to the Dempsey affair. The minister made a statement. I think hon. members will agree that the statement by the minister did not contribute much to the clarification of a very confused situation.
I should probably say at the outset, Mr. Speaker, that this affair, like the Ontario highways scandal and other such affairs that have developed in Canadian life, is due to a practice that has become fairly prevalent in Ontario. It may also be prevalent elsewhere. I refer to the practice of the government in power, whether provincial or federal, relying upon those who accept government contracts and those who profit from government business to finance their reelection to office.
That practice has become quite prevalent in Ontario, so prevalent, as a matter of fact, that while individual members personally 50433-234
The Budget-Mr. Noseworthy are not concerned or affected or involved in any way, and while cabinet ministers in provincial and federal parliaments are not personally involved, the party machine does become involved and those recipients of government favours, whether federal or provincial, receive what actually amounts to a quota which they are expected to meet when election time comes around. I think that is the practice which is back of much of the trouble we see in this Dempsey affair and in other such affairs.
My point in asking the minister the question-as a matter of fact my whole concern-was to give him an opportunity to clarify that confused situation. It is a matter of interest to the house because it affects every man in public life in Canada. Here is the situation. A member of a provincial legislature of some ten years' standing, apparently a reputable citizen, makes a statement to which he says he is prepared to take an oath. A cabinet minister, also a responsible citizen, categorically denies that statement. In effect, what we have is two men holding responsible positions in public life calling each other a liar.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that is a situation which is not conducive to good government. It serves to undermine public confidence in public men, in both the statements and the actions of those in public life throughout this country. In the interests of government, in the interests of those of us who are in public life, this situation requires more clarification than the minister has yet chosen to give it.
I realize that the minister is in a difficult position; I realize that he has much information on this particular case which he is prevented from giving to the public. I still think there are some things the minister could tell us that would clarify his own position in this matter. It is not good enough for two men in such honourable positions as these two gentlemen occupy just to be content with each saying that the other is making a false statement. Even though it might be so, at least one of them says he is prepared to take an oath regarding the truth of his statement.
This is a matter that should be looked into further. Whether it is the Prime Minister's responsibility, or whoever else's responsibility it is, in the interests of this government and of this parliament we should have some further enlightenment on just exactly what did take place.
For instance there is the statement in yesterday's Ottawa Citizen in which Mr. Dempsey outlined the time and place and circumstances under which the Minister of
3698	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Noseworthy National Revenue was alleged to have made a certain statement to him in which he indicated that the Department of National Revenue was quite prepared to forget the whole thing. The minister denies that categorically, and Mr. Dempsey comes back and says he is quite prepared to take his oath as to the truth of that statement.
This is all most confusing. While we in this house accept the minister's statement the Canadian public are not in the same position as members of this house, and they must be confused. As I have said already, the situation does not tend to inspire public confidence in men in public life.
There is another phase of this matter which I think needs clarification. I have no doubt the minister can give a satisfactory explanation if he wishes to do so. It is quite obvious from the knowledge we have that the minister was in possession of information that this donation had been made by Mr. Drohan. He came into the possession of that information shortly after Mr. Drohan's estate came up for settlement. The question we are asking is this. If that be so, why did the minister keep that information to himself for two years when the provincial treasurer, in the minister's own words, was legally entitled to it? Just why did he withhold that information from the provincial treasurer until a provincial election was called in Ontario and the person concerned is likely to be a candidate in a provincial riding?
If the minister was passing this information on to the provincial treasurer as Minister of National Revenue because there had been something irregular in relation to the payment of succession duties, there is no reason why that information should have been withheld for two years and then given out in the way the minister himself says it was given to the provincial treasurer when he was here in Ottawa to attend a conference a matter of some weeks ago.
On the other hand, if the minister's concern was that this man had violated the Ontario election act then it becomes more important that we should know why the information was withheld until after the announcement of an Ontario election. I think the minister owes it to the members of this house to tell us why that information was withheld from the provincial treasurer for a couple of years, and then imparted to him under such circumstances and at such time as I have indicated.
Otherwise, rightly or wrongly, the minister is bound to be accused of making use of information which he received as Minister of National Revenue for political purposes. That is the conclusion which is being drawn


across this country, that the Minister of National Revenue made use of information which came to him confidentially as Minister of National Revenue for political purposes, in order to defeat a candidate in a provincial election.
Personally I do not think for a moment that is the case, but I suggest once again that while this debate is proceeding the minister give us a statement in this house which will at least give some clarification to this situation.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on two matters which 1 think are of great importance, though they are widely separated in their content. I follow the hon. member for York South, who has again brought to the attention of this house the Dempsey case. I was most amazed at the incredible and amazing statement made by the Prime Minister this afternoon in connection with this incident.
I do not think since I came to the House of Commons in 1945 there has been a statement made which was so incredible. I say this because of some of the words which I think the Prime Minister used in the answer he gave to the questions which had been asked. One of the phrases he used was that this matter was of considerable partisan importance. It is more than of partisan importance, it is important to the whole parliamentary system we have here, and indeed to our democratic system.
There have been so many statements and counterstatements that I submit this house is entitled to an investigation committee to determine the merits of the case. On the one hand we have the former provincial member, Mr. Dempsey, who states that he spoke to the Minister of National Revenue and had the conversation which is reported in the Ottawa Citizen of May 11. The Minister of National Revenue denies it. Then we have the counterstatement by Mr. Dempsey that he is prepared to swear under oath that he is telling the truth, and that the statement he made to the press and which appears in the Ottawa Citizen is correct. In other words he admits that he committed an indiscretion. In my opinion if what Mr. Dempsey has said is true, then the Minister of National Revenue has committed an indiscretion, and I think we should get to the truth of the matter.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I accept what the minister has said, but I think that the country is entitled to an investigation in order to determine the truth in regard to this situation. I agree with the remarks of my deskmate, the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Zaplitny), who stated yesterday that under these conditions the minister should immediately resign. The right hon. Prime Minister, instead of being satisfied with this situation, should be tremendously interested, so much interested that he would be prepared to set up an investigating committee of this house to look into the whole matter. If the. minister himself is not prepared to resign, then the Prime Minister should ask for his resignation.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the other matter with which I wish to deal is one which I want to approach in the national interest. In the past the federal government under certain circumstances has declared national emergencies. During the past week we in the provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan have experienced one of the worst storms in our history. Indeed, in a report appearing in the Leader-Post the premier of Saskatchewan has stated that the affected area will be over 2 million acres of land, and that between 12,000 and
15.000	people will be affected. In addition there is considerable property damage. Some of the estimates in connection with the flood damage are that as many as 30,000 to
40.000	farmers will be affected, and that between 50 and 80 per cent of the farm land will not be put into crop this year in Saskatchewan.
We have endeavoured to get the Prime Minister to do exactly what he and this government have done on previous occasions, namely to call this situation a national emergency and have the federal government co-operate with the provinces affected in doing a job of reclamation and trying to correct some of the damage which has taken place. I feel that this incident probably points out, as never before in the history of Canada, that we need something done in this connection. I am going to suggest today that what we need in Canada is a national drainage and dike authority, planned on the basis of the Tennessee valley authority, because I am convinced that this problem is going to recur across the country. This is not an isolated case. It is not a case which we can be sure is not going to recur.
50433-234i

The Budget-Mr. E. G. McCullough In the province of Saskatchewan from whence I come we have, in the past few years, been experiencing more and more precipitation. There are tens of thousands of acres of our best farm land where the water table has been coming up and there is no proper drainage. We need a drainage system, not merely on a provincial basis but on a national basis, working with provincial authorities. I am suggesting that under a national authority a complete survey would be made to correct our drainage and diking problems.
Our presenl position in Saskatchewan is not something that can be solved by provincial expenditure alone or by any provincial survey, without taking into consideration the general picture in the western provinces. Some of the water that is draining into the province of Saskatchewan comes from the drainage basin of the Rocky mountains and passes through parts of our province into Manitoba. The terrific flood damage we are experiencing in Saskatchewan today is something which can well be declared a national emergency.
In this connection, before I proceed I want to indicate to the house that we in Saskatchewan are not asking something special for our province, but only something which has been done on previous occasions. Every member of the house will recollect that after the Fraser valley flood disaster in 1948 the federal government came into the picture and used federal funds in order to assist the provincial authorities to correct some of the damage. At that time there was an expenditure of provincial and federal moneys to the extent of $11,440,000. The federal government came into the picture and, under the arrangement it made, paid up to 75 per cent; the province came in and paid the other 25 per cent on some of the projects. Altogether as I stated, over $11 million was spent following that flood disaster.
Then of course, we had the greater Winnipeg flood, and set up the diking board with a total expenditure between the federal and provincial governments of $4,559,000. The federal government paid $3,419,000; the government of Manitoba, $1,139,000.
We have those two flood situations, and we have the other instances which were declared national emergencies in the Rimouski and Cabano fires. In addition we had "Hurricane Hazel" and "Hurricane Edna", where again federal funds were made available and federal authorities worked with the provinces in order to correct some of the damage and pay the losses. That is the way it should be in Canada. We are not isolated provinces;

The Budget-Mr. E. G. McCullough we are a family of provinces working as -a dominion. When one province suffers a catastrophe it is only right and proper that the federal government should step in and take some responsibility.
In connection with the-Saskatchewan situation, we now have in my own constituency a lake 10 miles long and three or four miles wide which was not there two weeks ago. That is a condition which is going to put hundreds of farmers throughout that area in the position that they will not be able to put in their crop this year. It has been suggested by members of this group that some sort of program should be undertaken to alleviate the situation.
These farmers are not going to be able to put in a crop, and they are not going to be able to pay their taxes. In the last few years the municipalities have been in a very bad financial situation resulting from the farmers not being able to pay taxes, because of the increased precipitation over the province. I have had reports from all over the province which have indicated that highways were inundated, bridges were out, telephone lines and other communications and power lines were destroyed, and in Qu'Appelle valley many cottages have been taken away with the flood.
I believe my appeal is on a fair basis, that the federal government take some responsibility in this situation and assist the municipalities and the province to correct this damage. I might say I do not feel that in the past we have had any authority in Canada adequate to meet such situations as we find existing at times in this country. I feel that the time has come for proper utilization of our land and for proper conservation and that we should have, as I indicated at the beginning of my speech, a joint national drainage and diking authority. This should be permanent and take into consideration in its surveys and work projects the watersheds throughout the Dominion of Canada and do the necessary diking, so we may utilize our farm land and make it possible to sow our crops year by year.
During the last by-election, when we were happy to re-elect the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce), I had occasion to be up in the interlake country, which again is very badly flooded. Many farmers in those areas will not be able to put in a crop this year. There is a situation which is isolated from the flood condition due to the storm in Saskatchewan. Nevertheless these are problems that are all tied together, and can be solved only by the co-operation of the provinces and the dominion government.
In the interlake country we have lake Winnipeg, lake Winnipegosis and lake Manitoba becoming higher and higher and flooding much of the valuable land in that district lying between those lakes. It is my feeling, Mr. Speaker-and I say this without any fear of contradiction-that if this problem were tackled through a proper drainage authority, and if a program were instituted by means of which, throughout Alberta, Manitoba and perhaps British Columbia that country and that watershed were properly drained to the appropriate bodies of water so we could utilize our land, we would not have these recurring flood damages.
If this government would see the problem and take the necessary initiative, I believe that, together with the provinces, they could work out an authority which could undertake this project. In Manitoba, if proper drainage and dredging were done on the Nelson river, as an example, and proper water control put into effect there, I believe that river would perhaps serve to lower the level of the lakes in Manitoba, such as lake Winnipeg and lake Winnipegosis, so we would have proper control and conservation in that area.
I am therefore going to plead with the government and with the Prime Minister. When he meets with the authorities from the provinces-and he has indicated that the meeting will take place on Monday-whether the damage is $50 million as has been estimated by some authorities in Saskatchewan, or whether it is double that amount, I hope the federal government will see fit to cooperate with our provinces so that not only in the province of Saskatchewan but throughout all of Canada we shall have a program to meet these recurring needs of our people.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have some
comments to make on this bill. The minister is quite correct when he says it was before the veterans affairs committee and was approved without amendment. However, I would call to the minister's attention the fact that this bill provides that any person joining the regular services with the intention of making the army, the navy or the air force his vocation in the future will be denied any of the rights contained in the several bills that set out certain benefits for the special force. Anyone entering the regular forces after July 1955 will no longer be eligible for any of these benefits; and particular emphasis is placed on the question of unemployment insurance.
All service personnel, up to July 1 of this year, are entitled to unemployment insurance if and when they leave the service. When this bill was before the veterans affairs committee the secretary of the Canadian Legion proposed that the bill should be amended to provide that in future members of the services should be considered on the same basis as those employed in industry; and if because of any unforeseen circumstances they did not continue in the services the length of time they had intended, they should be brought under the Unemployment Insurance Act in the way members of the special force are at this time. The exception was made that they should be brought in on a contributory basis, exactly the same as other employees in industry who come under the Unemployment Insurance Act.
At that time the committee did not wish to suggest any amendments for the simple reason that at least I felt that before bringing the regular forces under a contributory basis a study should be made to see whether the service personnel wanted to come in on that basis or not. However, there are arguments both ways. I merely wanted to say that our committee will recommend when the report is completed that the Department of National Defence and the Department of Labour, which have to do with the problem, should at least make an interdepartmental study of the matter to see first whether the service personnel want it on a contributory basis, and second whether it is feasible and practical to do the thing in the way suggested by the secretary of the Legion.

I know that the parliamentary assistant to the minister has that in mind. I hope that both he and the minister will continue to carry out what we have in our minds and what the Legion recommended, and what our report will recommend when it is completed. I merely wanted to put that on the record so that we would not forget it.

Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. member for Cape Breton South has very well expressed what the attitude of the committee was with reference to this bill. The bill has to do with the special force that served in Korea. Since most of these men have been discharged from the force or are back home, it was thought by the committee that it was not necessary for the situation regarding them to be as it has been.
As the hon. member for Cape Breton South said, we did hear representations from the Canadian Legion. I hold in my hand the recommendation of the Canadian Legion, and it might be well to place it on Hansard. The recommendation made by the Legion is as follows:
That the Department of National Defence make provision for members of the armed' forces to contribute to unemployment insurance so that they may benefit from the Unemployment Insurance Act in the same manner as do industrial employees.
You will note, Mr. Chairman, that the recommendation was that the Department of National Defence make provision, not the Department of Veterans Affairs. The recommendation was considered by the committee and was unanimously agreed to in that regard, that the bill as presented by the Department of Veterans Affairs be passed and that, as has been stated, the recommendation be put in our report that the Legion's suggestion be carried out.
I might say that I had already recommended that in the House of Commons when the bill was up for second reading. When we were in committee I was very pleased indeed to learn that the Legion thought along the same lines as I did. The situation has certainly changed, but as the Legion pointed out, many young men will be discharged from the army for various reasons before their time of service is up. Those who are taken on strength up to July 1 of this year will be in an entirely different position from those who are taken in after July 1. As I pointed out before, we shall have two types of men in the army, namely, those who, when they are discharged from the army, will have the benefit of the Unemployment Insurance Act, and those who will not have the benefit of the Unemployment Insurance Act.

In addition to that, a great many young men are leaving insurable employment and are going into the army. When these young men leave the army they will not have the advantage of the Unemployment Insurance Act.
Like the hon. member who has already spoken, I do hope that this matter will be given very serious consideration. Frankly, I think there is a great deal of merit in the recommendation of the Canadian Legion. When the hon. member for Hamilton West spoke on the unemployment bill the other day she also mentioned this matter of the soldier. Her suggestion was that the matter should be given careful consideration.
As far as the bill itself is concerned, Mr. Chairman, we are in entire agreement with its contents.
