speakeroldname: Mr. J. H. Dickey (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minisier of Defence Production):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING TRADE MARKS, QUALITY MARKS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Precious Metals Marking Act deals with articles of gold, silver, platinum and palladium, and in addition with articles plated with either gold or silver. Under the Precious Metals Marking Act it is not mandatory that articles of or plated with precious metals be marked as to their content of precious metal. However, the act does provide that, where reference is

Precious Metals Marking Act made to the precious metal content, that content must be shown in a particular manner. For example, a gold ring or a ring containing gold may be sold as a plain ring, but if reference is made to its gold content that gold content must be indicated. If it is represented as being of carat quality, say 10 carat, then it must be 10/24ths gold by weight. In addition, where such quality mark, that is the precious metal content, is placed on an article, the article must also carry a registered trade mark or a trade mark for which application for registration has been made.
The present bill provides for two amendments to the act. The first deals with the method of applying quality marks to gold filled or rolled gold plate bracelets or, as they are sometimes called, wrist watches which have base metal parts. The difference between gold filled and rolled gold plate lies mainly in the thickness of the gold or the other precious metal covering it. In the former, that is in the gold filled, it is 3/1000ths of an inch, and in the latter, that is rolled gold plate, it is lJ/lOOOths of an inch of gold which is of at least 10 carat quality.
Under the act as it stands, when all parts of a bracelet watch case have a gold content the quality mark and the trade mark can be applied to any part of the watch, but it is usually applied in the most convenient location, which is the back. Where some parts of the case are plated or filled and others are of base metal the quality marking under the present act must be applied to those parts which are plated and the words "base metal" must be applied to those which are base metal. With the present size of the bracelet or wrist watches, particularly ladies' watches, it is difficult to place marks on the plated parts without damage, and in addition if they are put on they are often so small as to be unreadable. As a result, few wrist watches today carry any quality marks, and any quality declaration governing them is usually shown on a tag attached to the watch.
To provide informative marking on a watch itself, it is proposed in this amendment that the manufacturer be permitted to indicate on the outer side of the base metal back the quality mark of the other parts of the watch with an indication of which parts are base metal. No change is necessary where all the parts are gold plated or gold filled. This is an additional method of marking and it has the approval of the Canadian Jewellers' Association.
The second amendment is of a technical nature and results from the necessity under the existing act of applying to precious metal articles a registered trade mark or one for


which application has been made under the Unfair Competition Act. The Trade Marks Act proclaimed on July 1, 1954, repealed the Unfair Competition Act. The new Trade Marks Act provided that registrations under the Unfair Competition Act are retained as such and applications for registration still pending under the old act are to be dealt with under that act.
However, apparently there is nothing in the new Trade Marks Act to provide that the trade mark or application made under the old act, that is the Unfair Competition Act, shall be deemed to have been made under the new act, which is the Trade Marks Act. It is the view of the law officers of the crown that the Precious Metals Marking Act should be amended to refer to trade marks as having been registered and to applications for trade mark as having been made under either act. That is the sole purpose of the technical amendment.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING TRADE MARKS, QUALITY MARKS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while we approve of and appreciate the steps which are now being taken to have articles made from precious metals more clearly defined, and while we approve also of the second amendment which is of a technical nature, I feel that a great opportunity has been missed by the government to introduce a Canadian hallmark. For centuries British and French gold and silver articles have had placed upon them a hallmark, but Canada has never adopted this practice.
A hallmark is really nothing more than a stamp placed on an article by some legally appointed officer after a test of that particular article has been made. It is usually referred to as a hallmark. Centuries ago the manufacturers of articles made from gold and silver-gold and silversmiths-used to take these articles to the hall of the guild of the goldsmiths-Goldsmith Hall as it is called-in London. There the test was made and the "touch" was given-that is the term which was then applied-by the appointed officers, who were at first the guild of goldsmiths and afterwards the worshipful company of goldsmiths. They placed their mark attesting to the quality of the metal in the particular article.
The hallmark of Great Britain and the hallmark of France have been of unquestionable integrity for many centuries, guaranteeing the quality of the particular article. One can find, if one looks back into history-and there have been a number of excellent books written on this question- that the guild of goldsmiths was first recognized in Europe in the twelfth century, and that as far back as 1300, in the reign

of Edward I, the question of the quantity and test of gold was laid down in accordance with an old statute which defines the "touch of Paris". The "touch of Paris" laid down that gold had to have 19-J portions as applied to 4f of the alloy then used, which was an alloy of copper and silver, in order to make the gold firmer.
Following that, in 1327, the charter was given to the worshipful company of goldsmiths in London and they were given the sole right of placing the mark or touch on British gold and silver. Hence comes the description, the "hallmark", as being, as I have already said, the mark or punch which was placed on these articles when they were literally carried to the hall of the goldsmiths. In 1363 in the reign of Edward III, in addition to the mark which was given by the goldsmiths company, a mark was placed on these articles showing the maker's name. All through those centuries, right from the twelfth century, there has been this definite stamp or hallmark placed on articles made from these precious metals.
The modern hallmark consists of four ciphers. Usually each cipher is enclosed in a small shield. The first is known as the maker's mark, which really is the mark of the maker. That mark is registered at the goldsmiths company or at the local assay office. It shows the maker of that particular article. The second is the hall or assay mark which shows the town or assay office which has tested the quality of the metal used in that article. It identifies the office at which the assaying was done and fixes the person responsible for the tests guaranteeing the quality of the metal used. The third imprint is the quality mark which shows in the case of gold whether it is 22, 18 or 14 carat, or whatever it may be. It shows the quantity of gold in relation to the alloys which may have been used. In the case of silver it shows perhaps that it is sterling silver, which indicates the amount of actual silver which is used in each troy pound. Sterling silver, I believe, is 11 ounces 10 pennyweight to each pound troy. Then there is the date mark. The date marks are of a complicated nature, working in cycles and in most cases using the letters of the alphabet. These date marks are of immense value to collectors of old silver and dealers in antiques. A dealer can tell at once whether a piece of old silver is Jacobean or Georgian silver, and he can tell by looking at the hallmark the date on which the article was manufactured, where it was manufactured, the actual quality which has been used, and the name of the maker of the article can be traced.
Precious Metals Marking Act
We have in Canada no legal hallmark. When the French goldsmiths and silversmiths first came to Canada they brought with them the habit of stamping their silver. I quote from a work entitled "The Old Silver of Quebec" by Traquair:
The French silversmiths who came to Canada brought with them the habit of stamping their work with their mark. This was a personal guarantee that the silver was of standard quality, but as there was no guild or assay office in Canada, they could not obtain the warden's mint or tax marks. They either used a personal mark, or left their work unmarked.
The English silversmiths who came into the province also continued to use their personal marks, but to these they sometimes added pseudo English marks.
During the French regime, the silversmiths of Quebec used marks of French provincial types- initials surrounded by a crown or a fleur-de-lis, and sometimes with a small badge. Any piece bearing a maker's mark of this kind, with no other marks, and which is of French character, is possibly the work of a French-Canadian silversmith.
As regards the practice followed by the English silversmiths in the province of Nova Scotia, I should like to quote from the work by Harry Piers and Donald Mackay entitled "Master Goldsmiths and Silversmiths of Nova Scotia":
We must remember that there have never been in Nova Scotia any legal "hallmarks", or doubtless in Canada generally. In the British Isles there have been strict laws regarding the marking of gold and silver, which had to be of a certain degree of purity, and which had to pay duty, before it could be sold. For this purpose assay offices were therefore established in various towns; each of these offices stamped with its neatly-cut dies, what were known as "hallmarks", or "plate marks" . . .
In Nova Scotia, on the contrary, we have never had any such statutory regulations; and silversmiths, when they began to operate here, assumed the practice, but without legal authority, of themselves, stamping on their productions, certain pseudo hallmarks which intentionally (more or less), resembled those of the Old Country.
If you examine the articles which are produced by certain Canadian manufacturers today, you will find that imitation hallmarks are placed on the article sold by such well known firms as Henry Birks where they are using a system similar to the recognized system in Great Britain and are stamping their articles so that the articles sold by Henry Birks can be identified, particularly as to the year in which those articles were manufactured. I feel that it would be a great help to the legitimate dealers in articles made from precious metals, and to the goldsmiths and the silversmiths of this country, if Canada adopted an official hallmark. To look far into the future, when undoubtedly there will be collectors of old silver, it would be a great help to the collectors of old Canadian silver if they could identify the year in which the particular articles were manufactured.

Precious Metals Marking Act
In my constituency there are quite a number of dealers in antique silver and other articles of that nature. I have had representations made to me as recently as during the Easter recess-before I knew that this bill was coming before the house at all- asking that some steps be taken to get the government to give consideration to the establishment of a Canadian hallmark as it would give them or their successors in the future an opportunity of comparing the Canadian article, and of identifying the year in which it was made; that hallmark to be along the same lines as the established rules which are now recognized by every dealer and collector of old silver as far as the hallmarking of British articles and French articles is concerned.
While I do not imagine it would be possible for the government to consider an amendment at this time, I repeat that I think the government has lost an opportunity by not bringing in an official Canadian hallmark. I suggest to the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Defence Production that consideration be given thereto at some future time and that -preferably at the next session of parliament-a bill be introduced to establish what may be described as a Canadian hallmark showing that every article has been tested at some assay office so that the real value of that article, plus the date and manufacturer's name, can be easily established.

maintopic: MUNICIPAL GRANTS ACT
subsubtopic: CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understand that it is proposed to have this bill go to a committee. In that event there will be no opportunity to make any comments on it except when the Speaker is in the chair. As I should like to make a few comments, I suppose I should make them now.
The thing that strikes me about this bill, Mr. Speaker, is that it is really, as one might say, on the fringe of a substantial problem. It does not pretend to deal with the problem. Indeed, in a way this bill is a rather ridiculous affair, in my opinion, because it is cheese-paring; its effect is trivial and yet it is in the right direction. I want to make one or two comments on the bill, on the way it has been dealt with and also on the rather broader municipal problem.
As I say, it is small. The amounts involved, having regard to our total tax situation, are trivial. I think the expected addition this year is something less than $2 million, bringing up to approximately $6 million the benefits to accrue under the legislation whereas the total real estate taxes collected by our municipalities last year were some $614 million. As I say, it is trivial in the extreme. Actually one would feel that is the way it is regarded because it has

been dealt with in a rather haphazard, helter-skelter manner by the government. In the speech from the throne we read:
A joint committee of both houses will he proposed to examine, in the light of the Municipal Grants Act and possible amendments thereto, the financial and other relationships of the government and the federal district commission with the city of Ottawa and neighbouring municipalities.
In answer to a question on that point from the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) said on May 6 last, as found at page 3515 of Hansard:
It is now the feeling of the government that there are so many committees in operation at this time considering matters of great importance that it would not be possible at this stage of the session to have a committee on the scale originally contemplated-
Perhaps partly because of the conference that is to take place in October this bill, in the contemplation of the government, seems to have shrunken greatly in importance. To continue with what the Prime Minister said: -that the municipal grants bill now before the house might therefore be referred to the banking and commerce committee as soon as second reading has been completed; and that there might be an opportunity before the close of the session to establish the joint committee with a view to laying the foundation for a wider examination of the work of the federal district commission at the next session.
The federal district commission will have to look after itself, but whether that is satisfactory to them they are best able to indicate. In any event, it seems to me to fall in with the impression I have received that the municipal grants bill is now regarded as mighty small potatoes, as indeed it is. Indeed, the actual amount involved is so small one might almost suggest having a tag day to get the money. It has become so trivial.
The other thing I do object to is that it is a kind of hairsplitting. The government refuses to do what I think is its plain duty, namely, to pay its taxes, and relies on ancient privileges going back, I suppose, to the days of the kings and even disregards the admonition of the Winnipeg Free Press, which suggests they might abandon this privilege altogether.
Having said that as to what I regard as the trivial and rather unworthy character of the bill, I want to ask you, Mr. Speaker, to consider for a moment what the dimensions of the municipal problem really are. I read now from the Globe and Mail of April 25 a report of a meeting of the Ontario municipalities represented by the association of mayors and reeves, which report has this to say:
The municipalities contend they are facing a financial crisis because they have been carrying the burden for matters they feel should be the
Municipal Grants Act
responsibility of other levels of government. The Ontario organization claims that approximately 10 per cent of expenditure by Ontario municipalities are for services that should not be their responsibility. If the municipal position were to be recognized it would relieve the communities of $33 million in costs for health and social welfare payments.
I wish the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) were here to find out that there is actually somebody else who considers they have burdens to bear in this connection. Next I wish to read a report from the Globe and Mail of April 23 datelined Quebec and quoting a statement made by the premier of Quebec, Mr. Duplessis. It reads:
For the agenda-fixing which is expected to be the main work of next week's meeting, he indicated he will urge inclusion of two main topics. First by far is the problem of fiscal relationships between the federal and provincial governments. Second is the general problem of municipal finances, and what the Quebec government regards as the necessity of providing municipal corporations with more sources of taxation revenue.
I want to stress that. I might also refer in passing to an interesting remark made by the premier of Manitoba who suggested that the municipalities should actually be present at the October conference. I confess I see difficulties in that, but at any rate it is worth mentioning because it shows that in his mind the problem is a very important one and one in which the position of the municipalities should certainly not be disregarded. I should like to quote very briefly from the submission to the government by the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities just because I think it would be worth having a short statement on the record. It reviews the principle that crown property should pay taxes and it has this to say:
. . . rigid adherence to the principle that crown property cannot be taxed had a threefold implication; 1. It meant that municipal governments had to provide services to properties from which no revenue could be extracted.
2.	It meant that the extent to which such property did not contribute to the cost of municipal services resulted in a narrowing of the base for municipal property taxation.
3.	It produced a situation wherein the municipal
taxpayers in those municipalities where there was considerable concentration of crown property and not the citizens of Canada as a whole, were required to pay the cost of municipal services rendered to such property.	[DOT]
Then there is this further word at page 21a of the report:
Consequently, the federation strongly recommends that the federal government consider, when the present qualifying formula is being revised, the provision of payment of grants in lieu of full municipal taxation on all federal crown property located within the boundaries of an incorporated municipality.
I do indeed urge the government to stop this hairsplitting and to deal with this matter

Municipal Grants Act properly, although it will only be a comparatively small contribution to the larger problem. But why, when these municipalities admittedly are already in difficulty, are they to be denied what I think any fair-minded man would say was a reasonable thing, namely, the payment of their taxes? To suggest that the federal government should not pay full taxes on their properties because they confer benefits on the municipality is an argument that could be made with respect to any private enterprise in a municipality. It likes to be there, it is there for its own reasons, but nevertheless it pays its way.
As I say, when you come down to the facts, we are now dealing with $2 million which is about one two-thousandth of our total expenditure and the matter becomes very small indeed. So far as any argument about ex gratia is concerned, if the legalists want to cling to that position let them at least pay the amount they should pay in taxes if they want to go on saying that it is still ex gratia.
I want to point out in passing the extraordinary relative lowering of the position of the municipalities in the last few years by reminding the house that in 1930 the dominion had 38 per cent of all taxes raised and the municipalities 39 per cent whereas in 1948 the dominion had 67 per cent and the municipalities 12 per cent. We on this side of the house have been attempting to assist the situation. We have been saying for a long time that the conference which is now about to take place should take place, and I want to refer to one or two things in that connection. In 1952 our amendment to the speech from the throne included the following:
(d)	To conduct inquiries in consultation with the provincial governments, so that necessary information may be available for the dominion and provincial governments to consider jointly a national health insurance program;
(e)	To reach agreement with the provincial governments in regard to a clearly defined reallocation of taxing powers so that the provincial governments and municipal councils may have adequate financial resources to carry out their rapidly increasing responsibilities.
Later, although I shall not set it out in detail, we moved several times with regard to the reduction of sales and excise taxes on the municipalities, and although something was done it was not nearly enough. As I have already indicated, the municipalities are keen that that should be carried further.
I would like to say a word about the forthcoming dominion-provincial meeting. There is no question that the position of the municipalities grows increasingly serious. They are called upon to assume burdens which previously they had not assumed. As I pointed


out, their share of the taxes raised is merely a fraction of what it used to be. And so, as we approach the conference called for October, we have to hope and believe that a broad view will be taken so that the municipalities may be given a liveable position, where they can discharge their duties properly, and where they do not have to go back constantly to the higher levels of government for what are regarded by those levels of government as virtual handouts.
The provinces have assisted generously in certain cases. The richer provinces have been able to do more along this line. We know that the province of Ontario has given a great deal to the municipalities. But on the other hand there are provinces which do not find that quite so easy; and it is going to call for a very statesmanlike view to deal with this matter in October.
After all, these mayors of municipalities who meet together are responsible people. Perhaps they are much closer to government and its realities than some other people are. I do suggest they should be treated seriously, and their needs seriously dealt with.
I do not think I shall take more of the time of the house. The bill will go to committee, and we shall there deal with the clauses which are amended, and do our best to make what we can of it. But, as I said at the outset, this is only tinkering with a situation which has got far beyond the tinkering stage; and we must all look with hope and expectation to a real grappling with the problem in October.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: MUNICIPAL GRANTS ACT
subsubtopic: CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure no one will vote against this bill. It makes a slight improvement in the formula under which grants are paid to municipalities in lieu of taxes. Even in this place we are grateful for small mercies.
When we get into committee on the bill there are some details concerning which questions will be asked. But even at this point I wish to state that we agree with the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) that this legislation is hardly a sufficient attack on the problems faced by the municipalities of this country. We all know of the excuses that are put forward as to why more consideration of the position of the municipalities cannot be given by the federal government. On some occasions it is pointed out that the municipalities are the creatures of the provinces and that, therefore, there cannot be direct dealings between the federal government and the municipalities. There is also the claim that the ancient right of the crown not to be taxed puts the federal government in a favoured position from which it can move only if it wishes to do so.

But, Mr. Speaker, surely the time has come when we should recognize the financial problem of our Canadian municipalities, both urban and rural, as a Canadian problem. Anything that is of concern to the people of this country as Canadians should be the concern of the federal government and the federal parliament. This legislation was a long time in coming, and it has taken still longer to get it improved, but I hope this legislation is an admission that here is a field which should be the proper concern of the federal government.
There are ways in which greater assistance could be rendered to the municipalities. This formula could be enlarged still further. There are other tax arrangements that could be made-for instance in the sales tax field- which could be of assistance to the municipalities.
Then, as has been pointed out many times, there is also the possibility of real assistance to the municipalities being made available by the federal government through the building of roads, highways and bridges. There is also the very important question, still unresolved, of federal aid to education. There is the further fact that real aid could be given to our municipalities and provinces under the general heading of health and welfare services.
Surely we all know-we have all said it in speeches throughout the country-that conditions in Canada have changed greatly since 1867. Our economy has changed. The whole base upon which our life is sustained today is totally different from what it was under the economic conditions of 1867; and it is no longer sensible or just to expect that the kind of services which, by the British North America Act of 1867, were made charges upon real estate taxation, can be carried by that same kind of taxation today. The problem of our municipalities is, I say, a Canadian problem that has to be faced; and I hope the government will give very serious consideration to it, and will realize that it has to go a great deal farther than is envisaged in this legislation.
It is significant that in the discussions which took place a couple of weeks ago in the railway committee room a number of those representing provincial governments dealt with this problem. In some instances municipal officials were in the delegations. I hope this means that at the federal-provincial conference this fall there will be a real examination of this important problem. After all, we should not get into the situation where the federal government, the provincial governments and the municipal governments are treating each other as though they were
Municipal Grants Act foreign powers. Rather, these are various spheres, various media, through which we try to organize our economy and our society for the good and welfare, for the health and wellbeing, and for the best possible standard of living for all our people.
I feel we should not allow these constitutional and procedural barriers to stand in the way of progress toward something better. Let us remember the important part of our Canadian life, the important part of our economy, which comes within the bounds of our various municipalities. We welcome this slight improvement; but it only scratches the surface of a very important problem to which we feel this federal government and the provincial governments in this country should address themselves more vigorously than has yet been the case.

maintopic: MUNICIPAL GRANTS ACT
subsubtopic: CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the proposed amendments commend themselves to the house as representing an improvement. My suggestion is that they might go farther. This problem is one aspect of a federal system. We are all familiar with it. In Canada we have three ranges of government, in fact, although only two ranges are sovereign governments. The federal government and the provincial governments are sovereign governments in their taxing powers under the British North America Act. As everyone knows, the municipalities are creatures of the provincial governments; but nevertheless they are forms of government, and very important forms of governments on the local level where they can be and are most effective, as has been recognized in this house in many pieces of legislation.
The larger problem of relationships of the federal government and the provinces is to be dealt with at a conference and I do not propose to discuss those larger problems, although they involve the municipalities very considerably because, as has been said, the municipalities now find themselves charged with greater responsibilities without corresponding means of providing the revenues with which to meet those responsibilities. It is to be hoped that this conference will take the position of the municipalities into account in whatever arrangements are made between the federal government and the provinces.
What I suggest here today, Mr. Speaker, is that one specific relationship of the dominion and the municipalities can be improved by this legislation, and that is the relationship of the dominion as a property owner in the municipalities. Let the federal

Municipal Grants Act
government accept the responsibility of property ownership as it accepts the benefits of property ownership in the municipalities of Canada. It seems to me that if it goes the full length in accepting its responsibilities, then it is meeting this problem as far as it can be dealt with as a tax problem of the municipalities. This bill does not go that far. It still gives the crown a preferred position as a property owner in the boundaries of every municipality. My suggestion is that in all fairness the crown, where it accepts the benefits of the municipal services which are made available to it, should assume the obligation of a property owner to the full extent.
I am not quarrelling with a reservation that appears in a clause of the bill which says that in assessing the value of crown property the ornamental features are not to be taken into account. I am not sure just what those ornamental features are. Perhaps we shall deal with this more fully when we get into committee. At times, one would be tempted to suggest that the assessment ought to be very substantial on crown property by reason of those ornamental features, because those features sometimes are not ornamental in the view of the citizens of the municipalities in which those properties have been built. However, that basically is I think a fair approach to this problem.
The crown as a property owner should accept the full responsibility of a property owner when it in fact accepts the benefits and privileges of ownership of property. It is a real problem for the municipality to service land which is not taxed. The Canada Year Book gives some interesting figures on the amount of exempt land that exists in the municipalities in the different provinces. It is astonishing how much land is exempt from taxation and from contribution to the services which the occupants of the land enjoy. Most of it is exempt because the exemption serves the purpose of the municipalities. It meets some of the municipal obligations with respect to education and so on to exempt schools and churches and other property from taxation. But the amount of exempt property seems to be on the increase rather than the contrary. In the province of Ontario, which I take as an example, and I quote from a table in the Canada Year Book for 1954 at page 1153, I find that from 1947 to 1951 the total assessable real property rose from $3 billion to $3,800 million, which is quite a substantial rise in four years. During the same period the assessed value of exempt property in Ontario rose from $639 million to $873 million. I cite these figures to indicate the extent of the effect on municipal finance of 
real property which does not have to pay real property taxes. In the case of Ontario, the house will see from the figures I have given that the assessed value of exempt property is 20 per cent of the assessed value of all taxable property in the province.
When one recalls that the great bulk of municipal revenue comes from real property taxes, the significance of these exemptions becomes apparent. My point simply is that the crown in the right of the dominion should not claim the exemptions which have been claimed in the past and which will still be claimed to some extent if this bill is passed.
If we take the year 1950, for which figures are available in the Canada Year Book, we shall find that the amount of taxes raised by municipalities in the whole of Canada was $574 million. That includes licences, contributions from public utilities, subsidies and other miscellaneous revenues of that kind. Of that amount the real estate tax was $400 million, which indicates the importance of real estate in municipal finance in meeting the problems of municipal government on its limited level. That $400 million on real estate may be compared with the total tax revenue of $478 million, if one excludes other revenues in the municipalities which are not properly called taxes. Taxes on real property amounted to $400 million out of $478 million in the year 1950.
The figures that I have cited for Ontario would apply to most of the other provinces of the dominion. In fact, it is a fair general statement to say that in all of the provinces of Canada the municipalities rely basically on the right to tax real property, although five of the provinces do exercise the right to tax personal property as well. They are the provinces of Alberta, Manitoba, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. But basically, real property bears the burden of municipal services. It is real property we are concerned with in this bill, and real property only. I take it that personal property does not enter into it.
If this measure is good in the direction in which it travels, it seems to me it would be good to go the whole way and have the crown assume the full responsibility on property with respect to municipal taxation.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, perhaps I should make a few very short general remarks at this point. First of all I should like to register a complaint as far as the Minister of Finance is concerned in his capacity as leader of the house, in that we had no notice yesterday of the fact that these estimates were going to be brought on this afternoon. As a matter of fact, I first heard of it at about 20 or 25 minutes past six. I know that a certain number of members of the house who were interested in bringing up certain questions with respect to this department perhaps had no notice that the estimates were to be dealt with at the present time. I think this is unfair to them. As far as I am concerned, I sat on the committee and had an opportunity to ask any question I wished, and so forth. But so far as the general membership of the house is concerned, estimates of any department should not be brought on without some prior notice. I understand that this situation arose because the legislation with which we were dealing this afternoon went through more rapidly than was expected, but I would hope that this sort of situation would not arise again-not that I am complaining about the rapiditv with which the


legislation went through. As everyone in the house knows, the committee on estimates had a considerable number of meetings dealing with the estimates of this department. There were in the neighbourhood of 11 or 12 meetings of some two hours or more duration each. During that time those of us who were on the committee had a full opportunity to ask any questions they wished. Officials of the department were there in large numbers, and perhaps larger numbers than will be the case with almost any other committee, owing to the fact that this department contains some six or more definite and distinct branches, each dealing with something which really in most cases has very little relationship to the other branches. As a result, the number of officials required to be present to answer questions was perhaps larger than would be the case with most departments.
At this point I should like to pay a tribute to the officials of the department who appeared before the committee. I believe that all of us who are on the committee were impressed with the ability of these officials, with the knowledge they displayed of their subject and with the way in which they gave their answers to the questions that were asked. Our coming into contact with these officials of this department did a good deal, as far as the members of the committee are concerned, to increase, shall I say, our confidence in the way in which the affairs of the department are being carried on by the civil servants whose duty it is to administer this department.
As I indicated previously, those of us who are on the committee had a full opportunity to ask all the questions that they had in mind and to which they wished to secure answers. Of course, the number of members on the committee is limited, and that essentially is the reason why these estimates need to be brought back into the house, so that other members who did not have that opportunity can bring up the subjects which particularly affect them and in which they are interested. Once more I regret that perhaps they have not had as much notice as they should-in fact, they have had no notice-so that they might be in a position to do that. As far as I am concerned, and perhaps also most of the other members of the committee, I have very few questions, if any, left to ask. From the point of view of the hon. members who did serve on that committee, I think that there is no question that sending the estimates to the committee will have served very greatly both to facilitate their passage in the house and to shorten the length of time it may take for discussion. Also, having dealt with these matters in the committee, it means that in most cases they

have received more thorough answers than would perhaps have been the case it we had dealt with them only in the house.
There is one other general matter about which I would like to say something. That is the general development of the north country. Perhaps all of us in Canada have been disappointed that our whole northern area-[DOT] you might say, practically the northern half of this country-which comprises the Northwest Territories and the Yukon Territory particularly coming within the purview of this department, but also, of course, the northern parts of the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, and Labrador, all that large area, has developed so slowly and has received so little attention. I do not place the responsibility for that on the present minister or on anyone in particular. It has unfortunately been the case right through our history, no matter what government was in power and no matter what minister was in charge of the northern affairs of this country, that very little attention really was paid to what went on in our north country, and very few real efforts were made to open up and develop that country.
There is no question that we need to bestir ourselves to a much greater extent than has been the case in the past if we are to make any real use of the northern half of this continent for our own people and thus to provide even, shall I say, a reasonable excuse for us as Canadians to continue to hold and administer that area. With the very considerable amount of overcrowding of population which exists in so many parts of the world, it is, without any need of demonstration, an anachronism that approximately one-quarter of this continent under our control and administration should contain at the present time something in the neighbourhood of 25,000 people.
It is an area which could support quite a large population, as evidenced by similar sorts of areas in Europe and Asia, areas which lie in the same degree of latitude and in many cases have much the same type of climatic conditions and so forth. The minister may say that the eastern Arctic is an extremely inhospitable area and is not capable of development in this way, that way or the other way/ I agree that that is probably the case as far as many parts of the eastern Arctic are concerned and that the best we can hope for is certain mineral developments and its use as a reindeer pasture or something else of that sort for the providing of meat. But the western Arctic is a very different proposition. There are possibilities for forestry and mining and-I do not think that there is any doubt about it-for oil development, agricultural development and
Supply-Northern Affairs so on in the western Arctic. In order to make that development possible, the essential thing-and I found there was no disagreement on this in the committee-is the provision of better methods of transportation.
In other words, before the country can be opened up, or before it can develop in any way to any great extent, we must have roads up into that country. In the committee I was disappointed to find that the amount of road building which is projected this year is almost negligible. It seems to me that this department should be taking a much more imaginative view of the possibilities of this north country, without counting particularly the cost of putting in a certain number of miles of road-whether it is 5 miles, 10 miles, 20 miles or 100 miles-at the present time and saying, "That is not going to pay for itself in the next year or two", and so forth. I think we must take a much longer term view than that and must begin to provide transportation facilities on a much broader scale than that on which they have been provided so far.
When the estimates of this department come down next year, instead of there being really nothing in the estimates to provide for road construction, except the provision for certain bridges to be built, I would hope that, considering the total amount of the budget we would have a reasonable provision for the building of roads in that area.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Like the hon. member who has just spoken, Mr. Chairman, I also had the privilege of serving on the committee on estimates and I should like to make a few general remarks at this time. When the affairs of this department were before the committee on estimates, I believe the consensus was that the minister was tackling the many problems of the Canadian north with conviction and courage, and we look for better things in the years to come.
In the committee there was an expressed feeling that sufficient emphasis was not being placed on northern development. We are all aware of the great potential wealth that is dormant in this part of our great country. There are huge resources in minerals, petroleum products and forest products. It has been shown quite conclusively to this committee that heavy expenditures will be necessary to develop access roads to the centres of raw materials and to provide railroads to solve the very acute problem of transportation. It is an economic question on which there is argument on both sides. There are those who say that it would be unwise to make the necessary heavy expenditures while more settled parts of Canada are crying for these same services. On the other hand,

Supply-Northern Affairs there are those who say that if we do not develop our great north, there are others who may take a more active role and beat us to it. As I say, this is just a matter of opinion and there is great argument on both sides. It is gratifying to know, however, that the minister is paying more attention to the north, that heavy outlays for survey and study are being made and that definite action will follow this planning.
The department, in co-operation with the Department of National Health and Welfare, is doing a vastly improved job in looking after the Indian and the Eskimo population. This is a great humane problem, and the sensible program to adopt, it seems to me, would be one that would provide facilities to make these people self-supporting. This seems to be the general plan that is being followed.
Efforts are also being made to improve the living conditions of all our people who, by necessity or by choice, live beyond our provincial territories. As proof of this statement, may I say that the federal government makes an annual average expenditure of approximately $1,500 per head of population for our northern Canadians whereas the over-all average expenditure in Canada is about $300.
I should like to say a few words about national parks. We have the Revelstoke and Glacier parks in the part of British Columbia that I represent and I am glad to see that a small expenditure-and it is a very small one-is being made this year. In comparison with the amount provided for other parks across Canada, we are certainly not being treated overgenerously. A larger program should be inaugurated to make these parks of more use to the citizens of the interior of British Columbia and to Canada generally.
I should like to suggest to the minister that the possibility of providing a road-even if it is open only in the summer months-into Glacier park might be studied more carefully. I would also suggest that the two parks could be united into one larger national park. Failing this, a road connecting the Revelstoke and Glacier parks and going on to Golden should be carefully studied. I am sure the government of British Columbia would be interested in this matter. Such a road I believe would be one of the most scenic in Canada, would prove to be a tourist attraction of great interest, and would be of great value to the Revelstoke and Okanagan areas.
I am glad to note that the question of federal-provincial co-operation in conservation and development of natural resources is being carefully studied and that this matter

will be discussed at greater length in a conference that is to be held later on this year. I hope this problem will be openly and carefully canvassed so that a program in the best interests of the provinces and of the people of Canada will be laid down for future guidance.
I could say something about the engineering and water resources branch of this department. However, in view of the problem that is being studied in another committee in this house at the present time, I think we shall leave until a later occasion any remarks on this subject.
In closing, Mr. Chairman, I would make the same plea that I have made on many occasions in this chamber, namely that the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources and the provinces work together harmoniously for the good of all.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I have only one or two comments to make on these particular estimates. I contend tonight, as I contended in the estimates committee, that Canada's northern development is lagging far behind that of other Arctic countries including Russia, Norway, Sweden, and Finland. According to the evidence which we were given in the estimates committee, and as emphasized by the hon. member for Calgary North tonight, the whole population of the Northwest Territories today is between 25,000 and 26,000 people. I think that number includes 7,000 Eskimos and about 4,000 Indians. In other words, since 1945 our population has increased very little, despite the expenditures of fairly substantial sums of money.
I think this parliament should realize that today in the north Canada has a real population vacuum. I am told that in Russia there are 50 cities each with a population of 50,000 or more. Whether the minister wants to admit it or not, I think it is fair to say that Russia and the Scandinavian countries are doing a much better job of opening up their north then we are doing. What is the reason for this lack of progress? As I see it the reason is fairly apparent. Both the Scandinavian countries and Russia are consciously and deliberately opening up their north on a planned basis. In Canada we are remaining virtually indifferent to our Arctic areas. This government's policy towards the Northwest Territories and the Yukon is a kind of "laissez-faire" policy, a "leave alone" policy. I think it lacks aggressiveness and imagination.
Let us look for a moment at the money we are proposing to spend on the north, as indicated by these estimates. According to

the estimates we are proposing to spend $7 million on northern development. That amount is about -16 per cent of our total budget. I contend that such a small amount is completely inadequate. I say it compares most unfavourably with what is being spent by other Arctic countries. I have a clipping in my hand from a recent issue of Time magazine which I quoted in the committee on estimates. I should like to read it to the house. It has to do with what Norway spent on her northern areas in the last year, and reads:
Norway, with less than a quarter of Canada's population, is now spending $40 million on the economic development of the Norwegian Arctic.
In other words, Canada, a far richer country than Norway and with an Arctic of far richer possibilities, is today spending on northern development less than one-fifth of the amount Norway is spending.
In my opinion one of the major weaknesses of the department is that it has no colonization policy. It has no particular plan to get settlers to move into northern Canada. Whether or not we want to admit it, social conditions on our frontiers are still very primitive. In most cases it is a case of the lone settler struggling against raw nature. I say these conditions are not good enough. The hon. member for Calgary North mentioned a highway program. I think it is shocking that in the whole Northwest Territories, Canada has only 130 miles of highway. Moreover I am told that many of these miles of highway are in poor shape. Apart from the Alaska highway, we only have 400 miles of highway in the Yukon. Surely it is time we started to open up that country.
As I said a moment ago, the Scandinavian countries and Russia have an over-all plan. They are opening up the northern parts of their countries on a planned basis. When they proceed to open up new areas they send in bulldozers first to clear the land. Then they send in carpenters to build houses, schools, theatres, stores and the like. Finally they move in the people. The minister said in the estimates committee that much of the Russian development is done by forced labour. I am quite prepared to admit that to a degree his statement may be true, but it is obviously not entirely correct. I do not think parliament should allow the Russian bogey to affect us to such an extent that we are not willing to learn from the progress they have made.
I think Dr. Stefansson is one of the best known explorers of the world's Arctic areas
Supply-Northern Affairs today. Not long ago he addressed the Canadian Club in Toronto and, as reported in the Toronto Globe and Mail, he had this to say:
. . . there is no real reason why large communities cannot be developed in Canada's north which are either fully self-sufficient or better integrated into the national economy. Dr. Stefansson, who has spent more than ten years of his life within the Polar circle, said it was a fallacy to suppose that agriculture, cattle and manufacture, could not be undertaken in the far north, though these activities might vary from the accustomed practices. Just this very sort of colonization has been successfully accomplished in the Soviet union . . .
I suggest that we are living in dangerous times. If we do not do something to colonize our north then, as has already been suggested, someone else may come along and do it for us. For purely defensive reasons we should be doing more to get people to go north. Because if Russia or any other country should suddenly decide to attack us from the north, they would go through those territories like a hot knife through butter. I say the time has come for the government to decide to spend more money on northern development, and to adopt a plan for colonizing the north. The time is rapidly approaching when some action must be taken.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I want to say a few words on the first item because in considering the estimates of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources I believe we are dealing with one of the most important departments in the whole gamut of government operations. It was my privilege to be a member of the estimates committee, and for the first time I had the opportunity of really becoming familiar with the possibilities of Canada's north that have been referred to by the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre. But in addition to northern affairs the other items we have before us tonight are, in my opinion, of equal importance because under this department we consider lands, water resources and forests. That just about covers everything of significance so far as our natural resources are concerned.
Then we also have to consider the national parks branch, under which come tourist activities which, as most hon. members know, are one of the largest sources of United States dollars. From that standpoint alone it is of tremendous commercial importance. As I said in the committee, I was inclined to agree with the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre that Canada has been somewhat deficient up to the present moment in developing its remote northern regions, particularly in the Yukon Territory and the Northwest Territories. I was astounded to discover, for example, that actually there has been an over-all population decline since 1901. In

Supply-Northern A fairs 1901 the total population of the districts of Mackenzie, Keewatin and Franklin, including Eskimo, Indian and white, was 20,129 whereas in 1951 the number had been reduced to 16,004.
The same pattern is evident in the Yukon Territory where in 1901 the population was 27,219 and in 1951 9,096. I was glad to learn from the discussions in the committee that since 1951 there has been an upward trend. That is a hopeful and encouraging sign for the future. Like the hon. member for Calgary North, I was also impressed by the enthusiasm and grasp of affairs displayed by the officials of the department who appeared before the committee. I say this particularly with reference to the deputy minister, who is a comparatively young man. He particularly seems to have an eye to the future so far as the potentials of the north are concerned. Recently he has been making statements in optimistic terms with reference to northern development. One occasion was on March 15, 1955, when he addressed the forest products research society. He foresaw a development of the north not unlike the development of western Canada and said that climate was not likely to be any obstacle. The deputy minister went on to point out that the five-month average temperature from November to March was more than two degrees warmer in Whitehorse, Yukon, than it was in Winnipeg. Those are encouraging words. I had my first opportunity last fall to have a brief glimpse at the community of Whitehorse in the Yukon Territory. I am sorry the hon. member for that district was not in the vicinity at the time because I had looked forward to seeing the area more extensively. However, I can say from firsthand experience on the occasion of my visit that certainly there should be tremendous development in the immediate future. With reference to the deputy minister's statement concerning development of the western prairies the northern territories are not the only regions in Canada that have been very slow in developing. I would suggest that before we can see the results suggested by the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre we will first have to fill up the wide open spaces in the midcontinental region of the prairies. I feel certain that before we can leapfrog into the Arctic regions we first have to meet the needs for industrial development and population growth in our three prairie provinces.
It is true that Russia and other European countries have moved ahead very quickly in exploiting the possibilities of their northern regions; but we must remember that, in the first instance, their population resources are much greater than ours and that, too, there
[Mr. Dinsdale.l

are certain climatic differences in that to some extent they are subject to the influence of the gulf stream and are able to approach the development of that area from the ocean rather than from the land area. On the other hand, in our northern region we are pretty well faced with a solid, frozen mass, so far as the ocean area is concerned. I suppose that is what accounts for the comparative coldness of climate in the city of Winnipeg, largely as a result of the indentation of Hudson bay deep into the interior of the Canadian section of the North American continent.
Returning to this problem of the development of the prairie region, in terms of land, forest and water resources, I should like to deal briefly with the continuing necessity for conservation and a co-ordinated and organized program in respect of the conservation of these basic resources to which I have referred. We had a discussion on this subject on February 16, I believe it was. Unfortunately that discussion took place on a Wednesday, which is a half-day in the House of Commons, and we were not able to carry it very far. I believe it is fundamentally important that we take immediate action to have a co-ordinated and organized conservation program that would embrace these three important resources which come under the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources.
We are forcibly reminded of the need for handling the water resources problem by the periodic floods that take place each year on the prairies. During recent days we have been hearing again of flood conditions in Saskatchewan and Manitoba. The water control problem has two sides to it. At certain stages in the water cycle we have drought, while at other periods in the cycle we are faced with surplus supplies of water. The two measures that have emerged in solving this problem have come as a result of one crisis or another, either a drought crisis or a flood crisis.
The Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, which does not come under the supervision of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources-and I must say there seems to be some confusion as to the respective responsibilities of that department and the Department of Agriculture in this connection -was organized to deal with a condition of drought. On the other hand, during periods of flooding we have certain dam developments to meet critical emergency situations.
I suggest that if we are going to deal with the problem of the control of our water resources we will have to do so, not on an emergency basis, but under a long-term plan,

with some over-all national co-ordination. During the discussion last February the usual difficulties connected with jurisdictional responsibility were raised. I am referring to the respective responsibilities of provincial and federal authorities. This seems to suggest that a topic of this kind might well be included in any dominion-provincial conference, such as is contemplated in the immediate future.
Moving to another aspect of this over-all conservation program, we are faced with the necessity of doing something about our forests. The preservation of our forests is basic in any over-all program of conservation. Actually, the history of Canada has been staged against a forest background. Certain progress has been made in connection with programs of reforestation; but, again, these have been on an unco-ordinated and individualistic basis.
I was interested in listening to a radio discussion the other night to note the emphasis placed in certain European countries upon the importance of wood stands in agricultural areas. In fact there are some farms, in countries like Sweden, which are actually forest farms; and in considering the sale value of such farms the wood stands hold a dominant position. Here in Canada, particularly in the western section, we place very little value on our wood stands. In fact the few wood stands we have in the prairie region to a great extent have been the result of man's activity, as he has attempted to deal with the problems of soil erosion and soil blowing that have occurred during the periodic water cycles of drought and flooding conditions.
I suggest the department might well provide leadership by means of educational programs and through the use of the various facilities in the department to encourage an individual approach to the problem of maintaining and preserving our forest reserves. Unless we do maintain a proper balance there can be no hope that we can meet successfully the continuing problem of soil erosion and the loss of our valuable land resources.
I should like to place one or two statistics on record in connection with this problem of the preservation of land resources. Up to the year 1941 western Canada had abandoned 4 million of its arable farm acres as a result of recurring drought. Then, between 1921 and 1940, 267,938 acres of land in Manitoba alone went out of cultivation, largely as a result of soil erosion. This came about as a result of drought, as I have indicated, and it also came about as a result of periodic flooding, because with the periodic recurrence of flooding there is a tendency
Supply-Northern Affairs to destroy the fertility of the soil; a reduction in the organic matter of the soil occurs and when the organic matter in the soil is reduced, then the workshop for the billions of bacteria, which in turn manufacture the elements essential to plant life, disappear.
In other older parts of the world we are made vividly aware of this problem, because of the desiccation of those lands. In some areas the desiccation has advanced to the extent of producing man-made deserts. We, even though we are blessed with limitless natural resources, cannot guarantee that that happy state of affairs will continue unless we take immediate action to have some national planning in regard to this problem.
To wind up this brief discussion, I should like to emphasize that in regard to northern affairs and national resources we must take a long-term view. We cannot overcome the deficiencies of the past in the north in the matter of a brief decade or even two decades. I was impressed with the attitude of the minister and his departmental officials as we considered those problems in committee, but these attitudes must now be carried into action. I should like to suggest once again that the land resources, the forest resources, the water resources, belong to the past; they belong to the present; they belong to future generations yet unborn, and we today have a responsibility as custodians of these God-given opportunities.
