In the next 20 years, if you and I look that far ahead, we shall see great developments, and if the opposition continues to advise the young minister and his department in the way that they have tonight I am sure it will be a splendid stimulant. It will be something like what was said of the Minister of Finance. It will be a shot in the arm.
What I rose to say, Mr. Chairman, was that we want the minister or some of his officials, when they are passing through Fort William next summer, to visit mount McKay. We think it should be a national park. I have tried to get it as a national park but I have just been beating the wind.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That is what you have been doing most of your life.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
The dominion tells me that the province must purchase mount McKay and then hand it over to the dominion government if they want it as a national park. So, between the two, I just fall to the ground. Mount McKay is one of the finest sights in Canada. I have travelled all across the country and I have seen some great scenery, but I have never seen men and women so awestruck as when they drive up to the top of mount McKay, pass a little bluff and then see that great panorama, that beautiful scenery. It just holds them spell-bound and they cannot get their breath for a minute. It is the greatest scenery in the world.
As I have said before, we have our water system away up there. You common people get your water from down below; we get our water from up above, 800 feet above the level of the city. We have the finest ski jump in Canada, the finest runs for slalom. We put on skiing championships that are second to none in Canada.
I tell the minister that it would bring money to Canada if we developed that area as a national park. Thank you for listening to me.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to take up much of the time of the committee on this matter, but I should like to bring to the attention of the minister an island in the middle of lake Erie. I did this last year. This island has a lot of snakes and a lot of pine trees on it. I gave a long history of this island last year and I do not intend to repeat it tonight. We are always accused of being repetitious in the house and I shall try to avoid that. However, as I said before, this island is called Long Point island. It consists of approximately 19,000 acres and is 

situated in the middle of lake Erie and stretches out from the Canadian shore.
At present, this island is owned by a corporation which is composed mostly of stockholders in the United States of America. The corporation operates a clubhouse on the island which the members visit very occasionally, usually in the duck-shooting season of the fall, and they employ a force of gamekeepers to act as a sort of private police to keep people off the island.
When the island was purchased around the year 1866, there was very little population in the southern part of Ontario, and it did not make much difference at that time. There has been a great increase in population in southern Ontario, and it is increasing at such a rate at the present time that summer resort spots are at a premium. People have to travel many miles over the week ends and this causes traffic deaths and traffic jams to get some place where they can enjoy the beauty and other advantages of our Canadian climate in the summertime. This island is readily accessible to the main centres of population in southwestern Ontario, such as Hamilton, London, Brantford, Galt, Kitchener, Woodstock, Tillsonburg, Stratford, and many other places. It is not more than an hour and a half's drive from any one of them.
If this island were to be made into a national park I am sure the summer resort problem would be overcome in that area. Wildlife, which has remained on the island in a virgin state, would be protected. There are trees and shrubs of various kinds and native plants on this island that are not found any place else. They are still in their native state. There are eagles on the island.
I mentioned previously that there are more snakes there than are found any place else in the world. There is also as well some of the best bass fishing and duck shooting to be found anywhere in North America. The bass are being greatly depleted every year. In fact, the catch is getting less and the size is getting smaller. If this island were taken over as a national park it would give an opportunity to the people of the country to enjoy these things in the future. Control could be exercised over the take of fish and the number of birds taken every fall.
I mentioned before, but perhaps it is not clear enough, that if this island is taken over as a national park the rights of the Long Point Company need not be completely taken away. They have looked after this valuable piece of property for nearly 100 years and in many ways have done quite well, but I suggest that a handful of people do not need 19,000 acres of land such as this right in the heart of the most thickly populated part of

Canada in order to go duck shooting. They could do very well with 1,000 or even 2,000 acres; they certainly do not need 19,000 acres.
There are one or two other clubs which have been there for many years and I think they might well be left alone also.
The government should consider the acquisition of this land as a national park. I know the minister is going to ask "Why the federal government?" He is going to ask why the department of northern affairs should be concerned in this matter. There are other parks operated by the federal government on lake Erie and on some of the other great lakes. As I have mentioned before, this island is about 20 miles long by about a mile or 2 miles wide and it stretches out toward the international boundary from the Canadian shore. The Department of Transport operates a lighthouse and lifesaving station at the end of the island, and I rather hope that in the not too distant future we will have a coastguard station there. Nothing of that nature exists at the moment but we can always hope.
I know perfectly well that the province of Ontario would have to acquire the land in the first place and then turn it over to the federal government, but there is no reason why the minister should not enter into negotiations with the provincial government with a view to making an agreement to acquire this land.
There is one thing that has come up which I think is worthy of note since I made my remarks in the house last year on this subject. I have mentioned that there are a great many resources on the island. There is a fine stand of timber and there are many native plants. It is true that the proprietors of this island employ private gamekeepers, but they are not able to look after fire protection.
Last summer part of the island was swept by fire which apparently had been set by some people who had landed by boat. The gamekeepers were unable to control the fire and a large part of the end of the island was burned over. Native stands of timber and other material were destroyed.
As the population increases in this part of the country more and more people will find their way to this island. If there is no fire protection what happened this summer may happen again and before we know it these valuable resources will be destroyed. We should take action before it is too late.
I do not think there is anything else I want to say at this time. I wanted to bring this to the attention of the minister in the hope that he will give the matter favourable consideration.
Supply-Northern Affairs

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in the
interests of economy I am not going to invite the minister to create a national park in any part of the riding which I represent. We have one or two prospective apartment house sites and if the minister could see his way clear to take them over it would probably settle a problem which is bothering the city council. There are so many beautiful places outside of Toronto that if the minister were to be given a free rein as he travels about the country there would be so much of it nationalized that there would be little left for the rest of us.
We do appreciate that this department deals with some very beautiful resources in the form of scenery, some most interesting resources in the form of historic monuments and sites, and it also has the tourist bureau which helps to bring people to enjoy all these resources. I have two or three brief comments to make and I do not think I will have much to say on these specific items.
As was pointed out in the committee, the tourist balance sheet is rather unfavourable. I am not saying that that is due to any lack of effort on the part of the tourist bureau, because I feel that Mr. Dolan and his staff are doing a good job; but the fact is that Canadians spent $380 million last year in the United States while Americans spent only $300 million in Canada, which leaves us with a debit balance of $80 million, a not inconsiderable item in a balance sheet. There is a lot of work to occupy the department in extending tourist activities and encouraging travel throughout our national parks and perhaps into our northland. It strikes me that there are many people in this crowded world who would enjoy the northland as a vacation ground in the future and perhaps they have not been invited to do that in the past.
A word as to highways. On a visit which I made to Yellowknife I found that they have only 18 miles of highway, but I was astonished to find that with their small population of some 3,000-I am not sure of the exact number-they have 38 taxicabs. There is no point in having any more highways because there is no place to go, but the 18 miles do serve that community well. It gives an opportunity to travel by taxi throughout the length and breadth of that famous gold mining camp.
I should like to say a word about the hydrometric services and flood warning activities of the department. It seems to me that there is much to be done in co-ordinating these activities with the meteorological services in order to give proper warning against such flood conditions as can be foretold. If the amount of rainfall were measured

Supply-Northern Affairs accurately I am sure that much loss of life could be prevented, and in this connection I would refer particularly to the flood which occurred in the Humber river valley.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Could I ask the co-operation of the hon. member to discuss this matter when the officers of the water resources branch are here.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I shall be glad to do that. I concur in what the hon. member for Calgary North has said. In the committee we were given an opportunity to find out about the work of this department and we received the greatest co-operation from the officials who were called there to give an account of their administration. I think the hon. member for Fort William went a little beyond what was implied in the remarks of the hon. member for Calgary North. I am sure that the minister does not expect loud praises from this side of the house, and I am confining my remarks to the officials of the department.
In the committee we were able to review thoroughly the work of this department and therefore it should be possible to approve the estimates in a very short time. We were not satisfied on every point. For example, some of us were concerned that a house for a superintendent should cost $32,000 when it did not seem to be any more substantial than a house costing $18,000 here, but by and large we did get our information and that is what the committee was for.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to call the attention of the minister to the necessity of a park near the largest city in Ontario, possibly the most important city in Canada. No doubt when the St. Lawrence seaway is completed the city of Toronto will be one of the major cities on the great lakes. We have at the present time the best opportunity for placing one of the best parks close to one of the large metropolitan centres that we will ever have. I would ask the minister to see the Minister of National Defence and arrange in some manner or other that the rifle ranges which are situated on the lake shore road running from Hamilton to Toronto be converted into a park. If that vast expanse of unbuilt-up land ever becomes industrialized we will have lost the last opportunity of putting close to the city of Toronto a park that that huge metropolis should have. It would be the only place where there is a beach on Lake Ontario. There are hundreds of acres there which are going to be abandoned, we hope, by the Department of National Defence in the next year. Before anything happens to that land, I would ask 

the minister to get in touch with the Minister of National Defence to see what could be done to salvage a most valuable piece of land and turn it into a park which would be appreciated by the thousands and thousands of people who live in both Toronto and Hamilton.
As long as Canada is a country, if this is done, this project will be appreciated more than almost anything we could do and certainly by more people. I would call that to the attention of the minister and ask him to use his usual forcefulness to see that this piece of ground is saved before it is built over and lost to the people for all time.
There is another matter which I should like to call to the minister's attention. I suggest that he find out whether something cannot be done to speed up some of the projects that we carry out in conjunction with the province. I should like to speak for a moment on the subject of the Conestogo dam.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Could I ask the co-operation of the hon. member? Would he defer his remarks on this subject until the officials from the water resources branch are with me? Hon. members will realize that there are so many details in the department that I cannot possibly know what point we have reached on such and such a work unless I have the proper officials of the branch here.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I shall be delighted to
acquiesce in the minister's request, and I certainly hope that he will acquiesce in my previous request as willingly.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I shall look into it very carefully.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I was delighted to hear an hon. member from outside the metropolitan Toronto area express such interest in our welfare.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: In the national welfare.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I am not sure whether it comes from the heart or whether it might have some connection with an election that is in the offing.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: We are not all political.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
In any case it is unusual that we have two hon. members from Toronto speaking tonight about areas in the far north. I too have had the opportunity over the last five years to visit the Northwest Territories a few times a year, and last summer I got as far as my hon. friend's riding in Yukon. I honestly believe that, before we can see the development of this country on the scale to which it is destined, it probably

will be necessary for all of us to see those far-flung areas. Only in that way can we realize the great potential that lies before us in this country's development. No matter what any other speaker has said tonight, the true development of the north can take place only with a sincere and real attempt to provide adequate transportation for those areas. In these remarks I am echoing the words of the hon. member for Mackenzie River (Mr. Hardie), whose long experience in transportation matters in that area has led him to make the same type of statement. When we talk about transportation in that area we must talk about air transportation, because, no matter where you go in those areas, the prices of the products which you buy are determined to a great extent by the cost which is tied up in the air transportation charges for getting the products there. In addition, of course, it is not going to be possible to induce the necessary population to go to that area unless there is easy access in and out.
The hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) mentioned his son's anxiety to return to civilization. I would probably frown on that remark in so far as it describes conditions. I think that the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Michener) was closer to the mark when he described some of the realities of Yellowknife and the fact that taxicabs are as numerous there as they are in the most populated cities in the southern areas. But at the same time we must recognize that, even in connection with population, it is necessary to see that easy movement of personnel is possible into and out of the northern areas.
How are we going to accomplish this? There are those who will say that it is probably necessary to subsidize some type of air transportation system. Frankly, I think we have waited so long that that period is now past and that the air operators of this country are in a position without help to provide the transportation which is required. I do not want to spend too much time on this particular phase of my remarks, because I hope to have a great deal more to say about this when we get to another department with which it is more vitally connected. But it seems to me that it is necessary for the government to provide at least a lead to the private air operators so that we will go ahead with the development which should take place. In other words, I do not think that transportation should lag behind; it should be in the forefront; and it is absolutely necessary that it should exist in order that proper development may take place. In connection with the policy which might be pursued, I should like to read a paragraph from "Civil Air Policy'' as enunciated in the United States 50433-235
Supply-Northern Affairs in a report by the air co-ordinating committee by direction of the President. Here are the words which are used in that report:
In determining policies appropriate to air transportation, it must be kept in mind that this is an industry affected with a public interest. The responsibility of the government, however, is not to carve out some predetermined role for air transportation and then attempt to force the industry into such development. Rather, the government must provide a general background of sound regulatory and promotional policies within which the industry itself will have the greatest possible opportunity for finding its own proper mission in competition with all other forms of transportation.
What has been the policy of our own government in this connection? It has carved out the fields and has told people more or less just what they will do with them. It is not possible to provide the expanding services on the basis of a policy which provides some type of monopoly east and west for a government-owned system and which has all aspects of the same type of monopolistic system north and south for one large operator. We should expect more than that. In reference to what we might expect, I should like to quote from an address by the Hon. Lionel Chevrier, then minister of transport, on November 10, 1952, to the Air Industries and Transport Association, in which he said this:
. . . with the substantial growth of traffic within Canada it is no longer necessary to insist on monopoly conditions with regard to regional scheduled services and government policy will not forbid the gradual development on a regional basis of a reasonable amount of competition between scheduled air services. Any such development must be based upon findings of public convenience and necessity as required by the Aeronautics Act and any changes made by the air transport board in this direction will be very gradual and related to maintenance of conditions which will establish a sound economic position for the operators while ensuring the services that the public require.
Yet since that date there has been no indication that any other policy is being pursued in connection with transportation in the north than a straight monopolistic policy.
There is now an opportunity that is being given to the north, and I hope that hon. members of the House of Commons will continually remind the government of it and will make sure that the north will have both the benefit and the advantage from it. In connection with the construction of the distant early warning line we are now engaged in probably the largest mass type of air transportation that has taken place anywhere in the world. It has involved the use of every available transport aircraft in Canada. It has involved the use of aircraft imported from other countries and it is involving the use of the aircraft of the air forces of both

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, here is a third Toronto member making an excursion into the north, as far north as Fort William, anyway.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That is not very far.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
We have had an interesting speech tonight from the hon. member for Fort William. The hon. member for Fort William might fairly claim-and I doubt that there would be many competitors-that he has administered more genuine adulation to members of the government than has anyone else in the short time I have been in the House of Commons. The hon. member not only praises ministers, but he praises anyone who looks like a minister, anyone who looks as though he might become a minister, anyone who has been a minister or anyone who is related to a minister. Tonight, however, I think he almost outdid himself.
In so far as the requirements of his calling would permit, he launched out into a criticism of us here in the opposition. The criticism was interesting. As far as I can make out, what he was criticizing us for is that we had ventured to suggest that rough people-people who could take it-should go north and live there. He described his own son-to whom I hope he did an injustice; I am sure he did so-as having gone to the north and come back, not able to take it but wanting to be snug in Fort William.
That raises an extremely serious question about the minister himself. I am sure he will not mind my being personal. I was interested in an article on the north last summer which depicted the minister. I regret to say that, not following the advice of the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek, the minister did not have a beard; he did not wear a hunting shirt; he did not have a knife stuck in his belt; and he did not have leggings. Indeed, he was just a dapper city slicker.
That is all very well. I must say that the writer of the article praised the minister for

being up in the north country, as I do. But I think that if he could only adopt the costume that I have suggested and the tonsorial arrangements which the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek has suggested, he would be even more convincing to those of us who follow with interest his excursions to the north.
I now want to say a word or two about a discussion which I find in the minutes of the estimates committee. I was one of the people who were accused of not being too enthusiastic about the estimates committee, but I find here an extremely interesting discussion and I wish to quote from it. It is to be found at page 438 and one of the new independent members who is not here at the moment was cross-examining the minister in a way which made me feel that he perhaps was fairly independent still. That was something that was very nice to think. As reported at page 438, we find this discussion:

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Yes. Mr. Minister, can you tell me roughly what the population in the Northwest Territories was at the end of the war and roughly what it is today? . . .

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: As to the population of the north, there are about 16,000 in the Northwest Territories and about 10,000 in the Yukon.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Then, what plans has the government got to encourage northern settlement? Obviously it is not having much success in getting people to go up there. Have you got any definite plan?
The answer of the minister is one that I find to be extremely interesting, and there are one or two more like it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
People will go up there when there are jobs and opportunities available.
To me that seems to be like saying that you will go in the water when you can swim; or it seems to be like saying that the hen comes before the egg or the egg comes before the hen, I am never quite sure which, but you never get anywhere. I read on:

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: But in Russia and these other places they are making jobs available.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
They are making jobs available mainly for forced labour.
That strikes me as a very interesting comment. I submit to the minister in all friendliness that that is a defeatist argument. Surely we would not like to admit that in a free country, where I am sure there are any number of people with the same kind of adventurous spirit they showed in other circumstances 12 or 15 years ago, these things cannot be done. It is not possible for me to believe that these things which are being done in Russia under forced conditions or under slavery conditions, cannot be done here if the conditions are made right. I read

on, and this is the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre again; I am all in favour of this independent member. I think he is very good so far:

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Well, Mr. Minister, is there any fixed policy which the government has to bring people to the north or try and get it settled?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
It is not a definite policy necessarily to bring people to the north, but it is a general policy ol encouraging economic development in the north which will bring up people.
Also, which is very important, it is a policy of using manpower possibilities that we have already in the north. I am thinking especially of the natives at the present time.
The minister nods his head, and I understand why. In a way, that is an unexceptionable statement, but on the other hand, when I go back to what the minister says about Russia, namely that we in Canada can do this thing when we force people to do it, it seems to me that there is a great contradiction between that and what he says later. First of all, he suggests that the reason we have not been able to get people to go there is that you have got to force them into it-

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: What is that?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
With regard to the
minister's remarks about Russia, I say that a fair implication of that first answer that I read is that we do not get people to go to the north because, in order to get them to go to the north, you have got to force them to go.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Oh, no.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I am drawing my inference.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: It is yours, and you can keep it. I do not agree with it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The minister can argue against it if he wishes to do so. I am just saying that, in answer to the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre when he speaks about people going north as in Russia, the minister says "They are making jobs available mainly for forced labour". Now I come back to the second point. This is to be found at page 439:

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Well, would it, Mr. Minister, be fair to describe the policy of the government at the moment as a kind of laissez-faire policy?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: It is definitely not a laissez-faire policy, it is an active and vigorous policy of bringing education to the north, and doing everything possible to reduce freight rates in order that the cost of living will be brought down and in order that further economic development may be stimulated by various measures.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Minister, there is no policy for colonizing the north at the moment?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Well, if colonization means settling people on farms, there is no possibility of colonizing except in the Mackenzie valley . . .
Supply-Northern Affairs
I am not going to read all that. I continue, later:

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
But we have a population vacuum in the north; are you doing anything to try and rectify it?
I am not going to detain the committee while I read at length. The minister makes answers which he will defend and which I think I understand, but I do suggest that as one reads this one comes away with the feeling that there is a great negation, and all the more because later on at page 440 the minister becomes rather mysterious and indicates there are certain things "cooking". That is my word, not his. I will read one sentence in the middle of the page. The minister is being questioned by the member for Calgary North. The passage reads:

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Well, in that case then you have no definite plans or even proposals at the present time for a railway from Grimshaw up into that northern area?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
No, it depends on quite a number of factors which are being discussed at the present time.
I am not going to pursue that now. 1 was interested in that conversation. We are on the first item, and I take it we will have a chance to ask further questions when we come to the relevant item. Am I correct, or is this the relevant item?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The relevant item would be item No. 312. That is where the development of the north was discussed at length in the committee.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: What item are we on now?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The first item of the department. We are on departmental administration.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: What number?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
The one I suggest is the first item under northern administration. In the meantime the hon. member will find a full statement of our policy respecting northland development and dealing with the problems of the north at page 535 and following of the report of the proceedings of the committee. At that time in the committee we were dealing with northern administration. The discussion the hon. member just referred to, from which he quoted a few extracts, was a discussion on the first item of the department. As a matter of fact, a full discussion of northland development took place when we reached northern administration, and it is reported on page 535 and the following pages of the proceedings of the committee.
While I am on my feet, I wish to thank all hon. members who have spoken for their suggestions and the appreciation they have

Supply-Northern Affairs expressed of the work of the department. I will be very careful to exclude myself, to please the hon. member for Greenwood. As I said, northland development was discussed to quite an extent by various members, and I do not believe I could add anything to what I said in the statement I made in the committee, to which I have just referred, in the answers I gave in the committee, and the answers that were also given by the officials of the department. There is this exception that at that time I said we could expect there would be a reduction in the rates for air transportation in the north. This reduction has been announced by Canadian Pacific Air Lines. I also said I was expecting a reduction in freight rates for water transportation. Since that time the Northern Transportation Company has announced certain substantial reductions in their rates.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: My remarks are going to be very brief inasmuch as I also had the privilege of serving on the estimates committee where all items of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources were discussed at length. It has been most gratifying to listen to the interesting remarks of the previous speakers. They go to prove beyond doubt that it is the considered opinion of hon. members, regardless of party affiliation, that every effort should be made to populate and industrialize the north country wherever possible.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have not
decided yet whether or not I will take much time.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Do you need some help?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: No, I do not need much help. I have had the pleasure on several occasions of drawing to the minister's attention the desirability of establishing a park in the region around the monument at Point Roberts. Recently the minister gave me to understand, and rightly so, that the monument itself comes under the department of northern affairs and technical surveys.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: No, not the department of northern affairs. The monument to which the hon. member refers comes under the jurisdiction of the international boundary commission, and the international boundary commission is under the jurisdiction of my colleague, the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys. This department has nothing to do with the monument my hon. friend has mentioned. I thought I had explained to the hon. member that we had nothing to do with that monument.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I used the wrong term. I was going to refer to the minister later with

respect to the desirability of creating a park in the area surrounding the monument. It would appear that the United States government has seen fit to take some 7 or 8 acres on their side of the monument for the purpose of creating a national park. We on the Canadian side are being told-at least, I was so informed as recently as three o'clock this afternoon-that the international commission is going to look after the monument because it is on the international boundary, which is quite understandable. They are going to clean up the brush around it and so on. However, it is going to be quite unsightly resting as it does on the boundary in view of the fact that the Americans are going to have a park in that particular area.
I strongly urge the minister to discuss this question with his colleague-there is not too much land involved-to see whether or not there is a possibility of creating a small park comparable in size with that on the United States side so that our part of the grounds will not look too shoddy compared with theirs. On the international boundary at Douglas the provincial government has a peace monument, and I must say it is certainly an outstanding piece of work. The minister has probably seen it. I am satisfied there is one of the finest parks there in the northwestern part of the continent. I would not expect anything quite so grandiose in the region surrounding the monument at Point Roberts. However, the monument is of such a historic nature, as the minister will realize and as his colleague realizes, that I feel if they could get together possibly something could be worked out whereby the people in the community could be satisfied and it could be made a part of the general tourist attractions on the lower mainland of British Columbia.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I am not entirely satisfied with the statement the minister gave us as to the policy of the department to populate northern Canada. As I said a moment ago, our population has been stationary since 1945. All the minister has said is that they have got Canadian Pacific Air Lines to lower transportation rates, and the Northern Transportation Company to lower freight rates.
Surely the department is not so bankrupt of ideas that they have not some kind of plan. Are we going on for another ten years without getting more people into our north country? I certainly think the minister should give the house a little more satisfaction before this first item is passed.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I refer the committee and the hon. member to pages 535 and following of the committee on estimates.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Oh, I was on the committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I gave full answers to all questions.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: But surely that is not satisfactory. Just because we put the estimates before a committee is no reason why the minister should come to the house and refuse to answer questions. The minister simply has not answered the questions which have been asked tonight, and before this item carries I think he should do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I do not believe I should use the time of the house in reading the reports of the committee on estimates.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Just tell us what your policy is.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: It is in the report, sir.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am not going to take much time-although we do not owe it to the house leader to push things through tonight, because he caught us by surprise when he brought forward this department, without notice.
So far as the minister is concerned, I think he will find that things will go reasonably well, in view of the fact that the department has already been before the committee on estimates. I was glad to hear the hon. member for Greenwood administer a rebuke to the hon. member for Fort William, who offers praise on all occasions and to everyone who happens to come within the orbit of his views. I would draw to the attention of the house the remarks of Mr. Adlai Stevenson who said that flattery is fine, if you don't inhale. Cabinet ministers opposite seem to acquire very early in life the bad habit of inhaling; so I think we should be careful about offering too much flattery.
Consequently I am not here to praise the minister. As a matter of fact-

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I never expected that from you, especially.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I was interested to note that the minister was somewhat disturbed when the hon. member for Greenwood drew an inference from his statement in the committee, because the minister is so ready to draw inferences from statements I made. I was glad to see the tables turned.
However, I was going to say that the committee on estimates was very interesting for this reason, that it shows how ridiculously easy it is to be a minister. You have, as this minister has, very competent and efficient staff officers who support you. And with such competent and efficient staff work in his department, so far as the minister is concerned his task must be extremely easy. It 's more difficult for us, who have to dig up
Supply-Northern Affairs our own information. Sometimes, if he is wise, he just keeps quiet and lets the officer of his department who knows the information give it.
However, as I have said, the staff of his department is very active and very competent. I do make this suggestion to the minister, that his is one of the very interesting departments of government. The minister recognizes that, as we all do. If on another occasion the estimates of this department are sent to the committee on estimates the minister should arrange for at least one or two meetings in a large committee room, such as the railway committee room, and there have on the wall one or two maps of the northern territory. Those maps should be large, so that we would have the picture completely before us while the committee was sitting. I grant that there is a very useful map published in the annual report of the department, but I am thinking of something of a good size, such as we now see in the railway committee room where there is a map of Canada showing thereon the railway lines. Of course it is only 30 years out of date; but, still, it is there, and it gives a picture of the country.
With the growing interest in the north country, I think something along these lines might very well be done. We could then follow on such a map the important things up for discussion when the estimates are before the committee. I have in mind questions of waterways, highways, air routes, mining developments, areas of population and things of that nature.
Similarly, so long as the department deals with the national parks, a map would be very useful in any discussion of that subject. It would take just a little imagination to offer a display that would attract attention to the work of this department, and I think it would be essential if our north country is to receive the attention it deserves.
I will conclude my remarks by repeating in part the criticism I offered when we were discussing the estimates of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, when I referred to the report that comes from the committee on estimates. I repeat this, because we find that unless we say things two or three times, no one pays any attention. My suggestion, again, is that if the committee on estimates meets another year and publishes a report, something in the nature of an index should be provided in connection with the report so that members of the house could find readily the information they require, and so that the minister, in his turn, could readily draw the attention of members to that information.

Supply-Northern Affairs

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
All I wish the minister to do is to take about ten seconds to answer the question I asked him. I would like to know what the government's policy is in connection with populating our northern country. I would like to know, if we spend the amount of money for which the minister is asking, if we will have any more people up there a year from now than we have today. I, for one, am not satisfied with the growth of our northern country since 1945. I would like to see something done that would encourage a lot more people to move up there.
I do not think I have asked a difficult question. What is the policy? What does the minister propose to do about it? If the department does not propose to do anything, then let him say so. But I do think the minister should answer the question.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I believe the only way we will get more people in the north, as I said in committee-and I was quoted by the hon. member for Greenwood- is to create an economic climate up in the north which will attract people to that area.
Let us not forget that, contrary to the situation in Norway, to which reference was made by the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre, our southern areas are not completely settled. In Norway, for instance, most of the timber resources are situated above the 60th parallel. A good part of the fishing in Norway is done above the 60th parallel. There is a pressure of population below that parallel that creates a necessity for the expanding population to go north.
But, as yet, we do not have that in Canada. It is only 50 years ago that real settlement began in our great western territory. The northern parts of the provinces are far from being exploited to their full capacity. It is only natural that the people of Canada, before moving farther to the north, will in that process of going north stop first at those places south of the 60th parallel where they can find some better possible economic advantage. Again, we do not have the pressure that they have in other countries. It is only by creating economic conditions that will attract people that we might expect a great increase in the population of the north. Unless we have a much greater pressure in the south we cannot expect a very large population in the north in the immediate years to come.
We have a population of about 15 million people in one of the largest countries of the world. A few years ago what was Canada but a thin red line of population along the United States border? It is only in very recent years that great thrusts have been made up
'Mr. Churchill.]
north in the development of our country. We have had iron ore development in northern Quebec.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: And in Labrador.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
And in Labrador; I am sorry. We have had the development of the Kirkland Lake and Abitibi regions in the northern parts of Ontario and Quebec; we have had the Lynn Lake development; we have had developments on lake Athabasca; we have had the Kitimat development. Well, these are in the provinces. I do not believe that between the 55th and the 60th parallel in the provinces there are proportionately very many more people than there are north of the 60th parallel. It is natural that the population should go up north as the necessity warrants it.
What we have had as developments in the north up to now that have attracted people other than the natives have been the mining developments only. That is where they are. As to other activities, I explained in the committee in very great detail the program of education and vocational training that we have for the natives in order to try to provide them with occupations in the north. I have said that we have prepared plans and we are studying the possibilities especially of improving transportation in the north, because transportation is the key to economic development, as the hon. member for Calgary North and others have said; not only air transportation, but land transportation which is very important for economic development and for the exploitation of the resources of the north. That is the key. But you do not accomplish that in a moment; it takes a certain time.
We started the settlement of the west 50 years ago, and it is far from being completed. That cannot be done in a few months; but I say that we have to see to it that there is transportation to the north at reasonable cost. When I was in the committee I said that we have intervened vis-a-vis the air lines and vis-a-vis the Northern Transportation Company.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Not very effective.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
A 20 per cent reduction and the freight rates diminished. That has been done since.
I said that we were studying and surveying road construction.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Before the minister goes on, may I ask one question. The minister said that we have been 50 years developing the Northwest Territories. He mentioned that 130 miles of highways had been built which

is less than three miles a year. Would he consider that that is the kind of development the people of Canada have the right to expect from the government?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I do not know where the hon. member gets the 50 years. Fifty years ago I was not born.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The minister said we have been developing the Northwest Territories for 50 years.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: No. I said we started the great development of the west 50 years ago but it was far from being fully settled yet. I was referring to the western provinces.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: There are still only 130 miles of highways in the whole of the Northwest Territories.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I did not say the Northwest Territories; I said western provinces. Moreover there are much more than 130 miles of highways north of the 60th parallel. There are a thousand miles in the Yukon, sir.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I am talking about the Northwest Territories.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
In the Northwest Territories there is a highway running from Grimshaw to Great Slave lake.
Normally, the means of transportation are those which are the most economic and suit the region best. Up to now the main economic means of transportation in the Northwest Territories have been the waterways, and they are still used to a great extent for heavy freight. As far as other transportation is concerned, it is the airways that are used. But there is a highway from Grimshaw to Great Slave lake, and we are now studying the possibility, following the suggestion made by the hon. member for Calgary North and the hon. member for Mackenzie River, of starting a highway from Hay River or somewhere on the Mackenzie highway to Mills lake farther down on the Mackenzie river.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Will the
minister not admit that the promised reduction in air freight rates came only after the threat of competition to the companies in question? Is that not true?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: No, I do not know about that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I am interested in transportation in the northern part of British Columbia. Would the minister be prepared to use his influence with his colleagues in respect to railway development leading to the north?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
The minister just mentioned a proposed road from Hay River to Mills lake. Can he tell the committee what difference that road would make in the length of
Supply-Northern Affairs the navigation season on the Mackenzie river? I believe it would mean a difference of six weeks or longer, would it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Approximately one month's difference, we hope.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Has the minister an answer to the question I asked him?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The department does not build railways in northern British Columbia.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I thank the minister for answering my question. I do not think it was a very good answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I do not agree with that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Regarding highways, I find that on page 445 of the evidence the minister was asked what highway construction had taken place in the Northwest Territories. I quote from the record. He answered:
About 130 miles in the Northwest Territories; and in the Yukon-the Yukon is more advanced as you know-over 400 miles, not including the Alaska highway.
The other point I want to make is this: 130 miles after years of development in the Northwest Territories is not a very good record for this government. It is time that they adopted a more aggressive policy on highway construction and other developments in the Northwest Territories.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I feel that this matter of populating the country is of vast importance, and I do not feel that the answers that have been given here tonight are adequate. I am sorry to say I have not had the chance to read through all the evidence given before the committee, but I want to say very firmly my understanding is that we are not inhibited in any way from asking questions in this committee of the whole house merely because it has been before the committee on estimates. Our rights are absolutely unimpaired in any way. We should resent it here very much if we are told to be good boys because a special committee has looked at it first.
I want to read from page 538 of the evidence. The minister referred me to page 535, where the report begins. I want to read from the top of page 538, which deals briefly with an aspect of immigration, stimulating of industries:
Economic development and increased defence activities is already bringing, and will continue to bring, opportunities for employment. At the same time, plans are proceeding for the stimulation of small industries, such as boat building, etc., which I mentioned a few moments ago. The natives will not, however, be able to take advantage of these and other opportunities unless they have some schooling. Primary schooling is the minimum requirement and vocational training is needed by

Supply-Northern Affairs many. Given the necessary education and training there is no reason why Eskimos and Indians cannot satisfactorily fill many of the jobs in northern Canada which would otherwise have to be undertaken by people brought in from the south, often at high cost.
That seems to me to be a self-destructive paragraph. First of all you say that you are stimulating industry, that the time will come when local people can man these industries. Then you go on to say that it takes a lot of time to do that. Does that mean that you are stimulating industry solely for the purpose of employing people there? Further back, if I remember rightly, you said that people would not go in until the going in was good, until the economic climate was good. It seems to me that there is kind of an impasse there. Are you going to stimulate industry solely for the local inhabitants and hope that what they do will be the means of bringing in other people? That does not seem to me to be very adequate.
I do not want to underestimate the difficulties but it seems to me, with all the unemployment we have, that for us to have people banging their heels down here if there is work to be done up there is most unsatisfactory.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: It is too bad the hon. member for Greenwood was not a member of the committee.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I am not so sure.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I made a trip to the north last summer and when I came back my deputy, my assistant deputy and I examined the situation closely. Contrary to what an hon. member of your party said, that I know nothing, I really learned quite a bit.
I came back with the conviction that there were two problems in the north. The one is economic, the problem of developing the north so that we can take advantage of the vast natural resources that exist there. I think the way to develop the north economically is to try to create an economic climate which is favourable to the development and exploitation of those resources. The key to that development is transportation.
There is a second problem, a human problem which faces the population up there. This is a most difficult problem. What the hon. member quoted a few moments ago was from the second part of my statement before the committee when I was dealing with the human problem which faces the natives. I dealt more specifically with the economic problem on pages 535, 536 and 537. On page 538, from which my hon. friend quoted, I was dealing with the human problem which faces the natives.

I was saying that we have to try to interest the natives in small industries. My expression may not have been the best, but I was referring to small industries and trades, teaching them to be carpenters, for instance. Then if we had to build a school in a community we would not have to import carpenters from Edmonton at great cost.
There was a separation of the two problems in my treatment and at that particular time I was dealing only with the human problem facing the natives.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I appreciate what the minister says. No one has anything but the most complete concurrence in the idea of doing everything possible for the natives, but that still leaves the question of whether there is a broader plan for development which can be brought about more quickly than the natives can do it, a plan which would have to be carried out by others.
My leader knows more about this than I do, but my understanding is that the development of northern Ontario was hastened by the operations of the geological survey. That survey did not go out prospecting to discover mines; what they did was to cover the geology of the country and indicate where prospecting might be good. I am not as familiar with that part of the country as the minister, but I assume that there must be huge undiscovered resources up there. I mention this only as an instance of the most fruitful co-operation between a government department and the most private and individual kind of private enterprise.
I do not want to see this item carried tonight, and the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre may still have other questions to ask. As I read the questions and answers earlier in the summary I felt that it was still worth while to discuss that all-important point.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The hon. member was dealing with prospecting and geological surveys-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I gave that only as an example.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Geological surveys are being carried on in the north in a very substantial way. These surveys come under the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. They will be carried on this year in the Queen Elizabeth islands. This is called the Franklin operation and was announced by the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys. Last year there were a number of survey parties around Baker lake, and also considerable survey work was carried out in the Yukon.
This work is going on all the time. My department is not the only department concerned with the north. The Department of

Mines and Technical Surveys sends out its geological survey parties; the Department of Transport has establishments in the north, and of course the Department of National Defence.
What we try to do in my department is to create an economic climate under reasonable terms of expenditure. I am sure the hon. member for Greenwood will agree that we should not go to the extent of creating an artificial development which would be more costly than sound economics would warrant. In order to create a favourable economic climate I said, and I repeat, that the first thing to do is to bring down the cost of operation and reduce the cost of living. We have attacked the problem of transportation costs and plans are under way to provide better means of transportation.
Other possibilities are being looked into, such as the allowance of longer time for depreciating the cost of power plants in the north. There is also one thing that is often thought of, but to which we have not yet
Supply-Northern Affairs been able to give a practical answer: would it be possible to adjust taxes on a basis which would have any relation to the parallel of latitude on which an industry is situated or where an individual lives? My hon. friend could answer that question much better than I could, in view of his experience, but I am afraid that he would not dare to go into that.
